1	# Jive Memory — standalone implementation handoff
2	
3	**Status:** proposed design; the service and Docker image have not been implemented or benchmarked.  
4	**Design revision:** 0.2. **Public TypeScript contract:** 0.1, reproduced in full below.  
5	**Deliverable:** one self-contained Docker image running as one container, exposing one HTTP port and using one persistent data directory.  
6	**Audience:** an implementation agent or engineer with no access to the originating conversation. This document is sufficient as the implementation brief; no earlier documents are required.
7	
8	## 1. The problem to solve
9	
10	Jive coordinates multiple agents and workflows that do work for a project or an entire business. Its integrations can connect to any domain: meetings, messaging, documents, calendars, customer relationships, sales, finance, staffing, operations, or software development. A business may have no code repositories, or hundreds. Several workflows must be able to use the same permitted knowledge rather than repeatedly reconstructing it in separate chat histories.
11	
12	The desired experience is: after an upstream change has been processed, an agent asks for context and receives prepared, source-backed knowledge quickly. It should not have to search live systems, read repositories again, or wait for another model to investigate the business every time it asks a question. Expensive understanding happens when evidence changes; ordinary reads retrieve the results of that work.
13	
14	This requires more than a document/vector store. The service must preserve entities, typed relationships, literal assertions, summaries, their exact evidence, and the dependencies that make previously prepared knowledge stale. It must support incremental updates, independent source revisions, historical views, shared use across workflows, and permission enforcement throughout retrieval.
15	
16	The service is not an omniscient model. A missing fact, an undeclared dependency, or an incorrect upstream extraction cannot be repaired merely by storing it in a graph. Retrieval must disclose gaps instead of silently launching an investigation or inventing answers.
17	
18	### Representative uses of the same service
19	
20	| Situation | Knowledge prepared upstream | What an authorized agent retrieves |
21	|---|---|---|
22	| Customer meeting | People, commitments, requested work, dates, transcript-backed summaries | What was promised, by whom, with supporting evidence |
23	| Relationship management | Organizations, contacts, ownership, interaction history | Who owns a relationship and what has changed |
24	| Business operations | Processes, assets, vendors, responsibilities, decisions | Relevant procedures, dependencies, and decision history |
25	| Software development | Repositories, packages, symbols, references, architecture explanations | Prepared technical context and bounded dependency paths across repositories |
26	
27	These are examples, not hard-coded database schemas. Entity types and predicates are namespaced strings supplied by adapters. Do not add a required `code`, `sales`, or other domain-specific core model.
28	
29	## 2. Non-negotiable boundaries
30	
31	### Jive owns
32	
33	External connectors and credentials; receiving events; schedules; workflow execution and retries; approvals and actions; deciding what to analyze; code checkout/compiler execution; generative extraction and summarization; answering the end user; and deciding when to recompute stale knowledge.
34	
35	An upstream **knowledge builder** is any Jive-invoked adapter that turns source evidence into the structured contributions defined below. A meeting extractor and a compiler-aware code adapter use the same write contract. Builders must submit exact support versions, not just unsourced prose. They may write evidence first and knowledge later, or publish both together.
36	
37	### This memory service owns
38	
39	Evidence persistence; graph persistence; idempotent atomic writes; version checks; dependency validation and invalidation; source-backed permission checks; search projections and local embedding encoding; readable-snapshot publication; bounded retrieval; exact stored evidence reads; and freshness/invalidations reporting.
40	
41	An internal indexing loop is storage maintenance, not another Jive workflow engine. It may render search text and encode embeddings. It must not fetch upstream systems, run business actions, or invoke generative extraction.
42	
43	### Deployment contract
44	
45	- **One image and one running container for the complete service.** The API, internal indexer, database, and local encoder are all included. Running the same image twice for different components does not meet this requirement.
46	- **One exposed HTTP port**, configured through `PORT`, default `8080`.
47	- **One persistent directory**, configured through `DATA_DIR`, default `/data`, containing database state and original evidence.
48	- No required external database, queue, object store, embedding API, model-download service, sidecar, Compose deployment, or cloud-specific integration.
49	- Host-neutral Linux container behavior: environment configuration, stdout/stderr logs, health endpoints, bounded shutdown, and a durable filesystem with the locking/fsync behavior required by the database.
50	- One active container owns a data directory. Multiple workflows and clients share its API; they do not each start a memory instance. Different businesses can run isolated instances of the same image with different volumes and credentials.
51	
52	A volume is persistent state, not another deployed service. The filesystem requirement means that an ephemeral-only runtime is insufficient for durable operation. Do not promise compatibility with every host or add a named hosting provider's restrictions to the architecture.
53	
54	## 3. Requirements and terms
55	
56	### 3.1 Terms
57	
58	**Business:** the ownership and security boundary for memory. The default deployment hosts one business, configured server-side. Projects and workflows within it are not separate copies of the graph.
59	
60	**Source:** a stable integration-defined object with an opaque head revision, such as a meeting, document, customer record, or repository branch. A source has a registered authorization policy and project labels.
61	
62	**Evidence item:** an immutable version of original source material, identified by `(sourceId, itemId, version)`. A source consists of items; a new source head need not change every item. Source URLs are citations, never instructions to fetch live data.
63	
64	**Entity:** an adapter-qualified identifier, such as a person, organization, asset, repository, package, or symbol. Names are not identities.
65	
66	**Assertion:** a typed relationship to another entity or a typed literal fact, with a stance and optional real-world validity interval. A proposal is not an implemented decision; a negated claim is not an affirmative edge.
67	
68	**Contribution:** an immutable, versioned unit of prepared knowledge containing entities, assertions, and/or summaries. All of its contents depend on all of its listed supports. Separate independently supported claims into different contributions.
69	
70	**Support graph:** dependencies from contributions to exact evidence or contribution versions. It must be acyclic and terminate in evidence. The business relationship graph is different and may contain cycles.
71	
72	**Snapshot:** a store-issued identity for a coherent knowledge state. It records independent source heads; it is not one Git commit for an entire organization.
73	
74	**Canonical state versus readable state:** accepted writes and invalidations can be ahead of finished search projections. Persisted knowledge is not automatically fully searchable.
75	
76	### 3.2 Required behavior
77	
78	| ID | Requirement |
79	|---|---|
80	| R1 | Preserve evidence, entity descriptions, assertions, summaries, provenance basis, producer identity, and exact support versions. Imported/compiler-derived structure is not rewritten by an LLM. |
81	| R2 | Share permitted knowledge across projects, agents, and workflows in a business; isolate businesses and enforce source permissions on all read and write paths. |
82	| R3 | Apply only changed/removed items; unchanged item versions survive source-head updates. Reject out-of-order conflicting writes through expected-head/version checks. |
83	| R4 | Accept evidence-only, knowledge-only, or combined atomic batches. Duplicate requests are idempotent; conflicting reuse of an idempotency key is rejected. |
84	| R5 | Atomically invalidate all declared transitive dependents of changed/removed supports. Preserve unrelated knowledge and other sources' independent contributions. |
85	| R6 | Reject delayed contributions based on superseded supports. Never silently return superseded knowledge as current during index lag. |
86	| R7 | Preserve source revision, store knowledge time, and assertion world-validity time as distinct concepts. Historical reads apply current authorization. |
87	| R8 | Support text relevance retrieval and explicit bounded graph traversal; return prepared context, citations, source heads, and gaps, not a generated answer. |
88	| R9 | Ordinary queries do not call connectors, read checkouts, parse source code, run extraction, or call generative models. Local query encoding or a caller-supplied compatible vector is allowed. |
89	| R10 | Expose indexed revisions, publication readiness, and paged invalidations so Jive can schedule work. Do not claim to know remote revisions that Jive has not submitted. |
90	| R11 | Serve the whole memory service from the single image/container contract in section 2, with restart persistence and no required outbound runtime connection. |
91	| R12 | Prove correctness with both non-code and code-shaped fixtures; measure performance and recall under realistic scale and permission fragmentation. |
92	
93	Contradictions can coexist. A timestamp or retrieval score does not decide which assertion is true. Human/model/compiler provenance is retained, but provenance labels are not proof of correctness by themselves.
94	
95	### 3.3 Explicitly out of scope
96	
97	Building Jive's connector catalog, workflow engine, live meeting transcription, production language indexers, generative knowledge builders, autonomous actions, or an answer-generating chatbot. Also excluded from the first release: automatic entity merging, arbitrary natural-language-to-SQL planning, cross-business sharing, multi-region replication, and distributed high availability.
98	
99	An adapter can still use SCIP for code or another extraction framework for business material upstream. Neither is mandatory inside the storage image. Do not confuse “the adapter is outside the storage service” with removing its role from the overall system.
100	
101	## 4. Implementation decision
102	
103	Implement a **TypeScript/Fastify application with PostgreSQL and pgvector bundled inside the same image**. Store original evidence files in its persistent directory. Bundle a local embedding model so indexing and text queries need no inference service.
104	
105	The graph is represented by entity, assertion, and dependency tables with indexed adjacency lookups. All canonical revisions, support relationships, invalidations, policies, and snapshots are in the same transactional database. This avoids synchronizing a graph database, a metadata database, and an external vector store merely to implement one atomic write.
106	
107	| Component | Selected technology | Implementation work |
108	|---|---|---|
109	| API and SDK | TypeScript; Node.js 24 LTS; Fastify | JSON validation, HTTP routes, authentication, errors, budgets, SDK |
110	| Database | PostgreSQL 18, private process inside the container | Schema, transactions, historical intervals, permissions, dependency queries |
111	| Database access | `pg` / node-postgres; parameterized SQL; versioned SQL migrations | Explicit checked-out-client transaction boundaries |
112	| Retrieval indexes | PostgreSQL full-text GIN indexes and pgvector | Prepared search units, exact reference retrieval, measured approximate optimization |
113	| Local embeddings | `@huggingface/transformers`; ONNX weights for `Xenova/multilingual-e5-small` | Offline model loading, rendering/chunking, encoding, versioned vector spaces |
114	| Evidence bytes | Local immutable files under `/data/evidence`; metadata and small text in PostgreSQL | Checksums, authorized reads, staging, garbage collection, backup consistency |
115	| Process lifecycle | Tini plus an image-local lifecycle coordinator | Initialization, start ordering, signal handling, child failure, shutdown |
116	| Tests | Node's test runner, TypeScript compiler, fixture/load tools in this repository | Correctness, HTTP, restart, security, offline operation, performance |
117	
118	Node 24 is a documented LTS line; Fastify has schema-based validation; node-postgres requires transaction statements to use the same client. [S1–S3] PostgreSQL has recursive queries, row security, and full-text indexes; pgvector supports exact and approximate vector retrieval. These primitives do **not** themselves implement this contract. [S4–S7]
119	
120	The model repository documents Transformers.js-compatible ONNX weights. Model quality and CPU latency remain evaluation questions, not reasons to claim instantaneous answers. [S8]
121	
122	### Packaging decision and its tradeoff
123	
124	Bundle the real PostgreSQL server; do not replace it with an unrelated embedded database merely to reduce the process count. One image does not require one operating-system process. Docker documents multi-process containers while generally recommending separating concerns; this design deliberately prioritizes the requested self-contained deployment unit. [S9]
125	
126	The API and indexer share deployment resources with the database. They cannot scale or upgrade independently in this release. This is a single-node service, not a highly available distributed database. Packaging makes it deployable as one unit; it does not eliminate database lifecycle, backup, or resource-management work.
127	
128	Do not introduce Graphiti, Zep, Mem0, Letta, or Neo4j as a mandatory backend without demonstrating the exact atomicity, support-version, history, and authorization guarantees here. This design implements the storage contract directly; it makes no claim that one of those products is a drop-in implementation. A storage engine change requires a documented decision and the same acceptance suite, not a weakened interface.
129	
130	## 5. Architecture and component ownership
131	
132	```text
133	Jive, outside the image
134	  connectors / workflows / knowledge builders / agents
135	                 |
136	                 | authenticated HTTP
137	                 v
138	+---------------- ONE CONTAINER ---------------------+
139	| Tini + lifecycle coordinator                       |
140	|                                                    |
141	| API process                                        |
142	|   auth + validation + four memory methods           |
143	|   writer / provenance / reader / evidence / admin   |
144	|   local query-encoding worker                      |
145	|                                                    |
146	| Internal indexer process                           |
147	|   durable index jobs + local passage encoder       |
148	|                                                    |
149	| Private PostgreSQL 18 + pgvector                    |
150	|   Unix-domain socket only; no public database port  |
151	|                                                    |
152	| /data/postgres     canonical data, indexes, WAL      |
153	| /data/evidence     immutable original payloads      |
154	| /data/staging      incomplete uploads/imports       |
155	| /data/instance     identity and protected state     |
156	| /opt/jive/models   immutable model assets in image   |
157	+----------------------------------------------------+
158	                 |
159	          one durable /data mount
160	```
161	
162	These modules are **to be built**, not separate services or existing packages:
163	
164	- `api`: routes, validation, authenticated context, rate/size limits, safe error mapping.
165	- `writer`: idempotency, source/contribution compare-and-swap, canonical transactions, snapshots.
166	- `provenance`: support validation, reverse invalidation, leaf-source inheritance, cycle checks.
167	- `reader`: view resolution, permission-filtered relevance lookup, graph steps, context assembly.
168	- `indexer`: deterministic search rendering, local embeddings, retryable index jobs, publication.
169	- `evidence`: immutable payload storage, bounded reads, upload transport, authorized streaming.
170	- `control`: principals, source policies, instance configuration, audit, maintenance, retention.
171	- `lifecycle`: start/stop sequencing, private PostgreSQL setup, migrations, readiness.
172	- `sdk`: the four-method TypeScript client. No business workflow implementation belongs here.
173	
174	## 6. Complete public TypeScript interface
175	
176	Copy this block to `packages/contract/src/index.ts`. It is the complete v0.1 contract, not an illustrative subset. Preserve it; the semantics in the following sections resolve implementation details without silently changing its types. Additional transport and administrative endpoints are separate from the four-method knowledge interface.

411	
412	## 7. Contract semantics the agent must implement
413	
414	### Identity, provenance, and writes
415	
416	A client is bound to a verified principal and the service's business ID. There is no caller-trusted `businessId` or permissions field in a memory request. `projectIds` filter relevance; they do not grant access.
417	
418	Source heads are opaque. `expectedHead: null` creates a source; another value must exactly match its current head. Jive, not this service, decides Git ancestry or whether a source rewind is intentional. A tombstoned source retains its last head for future compare-and-swap; only an authorized patch can reactivate it.
419	
420	Contribution heads retain their last version even when stale or retracted. Replacing a known contribution requires that exact head version. New IDs use `expectedVersion: null`. A replacement must use a new immutable version, except that an exact already-current no-op can be acknowledged without changing visibility. Reintroducing a previously superseded contribution version is rejected: publish a newly revalidated version instead. Evidence item versions may reappear when their original bytes and metadata are identical, but old stale contributions do not resurrect automatically.
421	
422	Hash the canonical JSON representation of every immutable version. Reusing a version ID for different contents is `INVALID_INPUT`; reusing an idempotency key for different batch content is `IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT`. Scope idempotency by business and authenticated writer principal. Retries with the same content return the original receipt, not a new snapshot. Reauthorize replay; deny an old receipt whose information is no longer permitted.
423	
424	Each contribution's support list is an AND, not an OR. A summary based on sources A and B requires both. Independent evidence for the same claim belongs in separate contributions. Knowledge builders must include dependencies on information they used, including cross-repository interfaces and lower-level summaries. The store cannot invalidate an undeclared dependency.
425	
426	### Temporal semantics
427	
428	Use three independent values:
429	
430	1. The adapter's opaque source head and immutable evidence/contribution versions.
431	2. The store's ordered knowledge sequence and recorded knowledge timestamp.
432	3. An assertion's optional `validTime` in the represented world.
433	
434	Visibility intervals in storage are half-open: `[from_seq, to_seq)`. An absent end is open-ended. `validTime` also uses a half-open interval; missing bounds are unspecified. Do not interpret missing dates as proof that a claim is eternally true.
435	
436	`known-at` selects the last canonical snapshot at or before the supplied store-recorded time. That snapshot must be published or the request fails with `INDEX_NOT_READY`. Do not silently choose an older published snapshot. The store timestamp is assigned under the write lock as an ordered record time; `committedAt` is returned only after durable commit, not claimed to be a hardware-exact transaction commit instant.
437	
438	For `validAt`, return only whole contributions whose own dated assertions and support assertions do not exclude the requested time. Leave undated assertions undated. Builders should split claims with different validity intervals; a mixed contribution may conservatively be excluded. This filter describes validity of stored claims, not truth adjudication.
439	
440	### Snapshot versus current safety
441	
442	`latest-indexed` chooses the latest completely published snapshot, but masks any of its contributions no longer current in canonical state at the read's authorization/consistency point. This is a coherent snapshot minus explicitly disclosed safety gaps, never a mixture containing newer, unpublished knowledge. Its returned source heads are the snapshot's heads, not falsely advanced canonical heads.
443	
444	An explicit `snapshot` or `known-at` view evaluates contribution state at that snapshot. It still applies present permissions and purge rules. A previously current contribution may therefore be historically readable after it becomes stale, but not after its source access is revoked.
445	
446	`includeStale: true` permits contributions marked stale at the selected view, and latest-view safety masking may instead label such entries `stale`; it never overrides access control, includes retracted records as active knowledge, or authorizes purged material.
447	
448	### Query scope and output
449	
450	Source/project filters match a contribution when at least one of its leaf sources is in scope. When both filter kinds are supplied, both conditions must hold. The caller must still be authorized for **every** supporting source. Thus a permitted cross-project claim may cite an additional permitted project. An empty supplied filter array matches nothing; an absent filter imposes no relevance restriction.
451	
452	Return whole immutable contribution versions. Do not truncate a contribution internally or silently rewrite it under the same version. A matching relationship may cause its whole contribution to be returned, so adapters should keep contributions small. Preserve `basis`, `stance`, dates, producer, and supports.
453	
454	`score` is a retrieval rank only. A graph query's `steps` are a typed path program, not natural-language instructions or caller-supplied SQL. Predicate lists must be explicit and nonempty. Zero steps means return authorized entity descriptions and summaries for the starting IDs. Returned claims must preserve negation/proposal labels; do not translate them into affirmative business relationships.
455	
456	Budgets apply to the complete context payload, not just summary prose. Use the pinned bundled model tokenizer for the service-defined token budget (not a claim to match every consuming LLM), counting without truncation; also enforce byte, expansion, provenance, and query-time caps. If a selected contribution cannot fit together with required citation context, omit it and return `truncated`/`budget-exhausted`. Do not represent a budget limit as “no such fact exists.”
457	
458	`readEvidence` pages whole evidence items, not byte slices. Large payloads use a blob reference and an authorized streaming endpoint. An individual inline item exceeding the page budget fails with `BUDGET_EXCEEDED`; it must not create an endless empty-page cursor.
459	
460	`status.sources` means canonical persisted heads. `retrieve.sourceHeads` means the returned readable view. `status` is not an acknowledged work queue; stale invalidations remain visible until replacement/retraction. New evidence without any existing contributions need not create invalidations: Jive knows it has first-time extraction work to perform.
461	
462	## 8. HTTP transport, authentication, and control plane
463	
464	### Data routes
465	
466	| Route | Request | Success body |
467	|---|---|---|
468	| `POST /v1/memory/apply` | `MemoryBatch` | `WriteReceipt` |
469	| `POST /v1/memory/retrieve` | `ContextQuery` | `ContextBundle` |
470	| `POST /v1/memory/read-evidence` | `EvidenceQuery` | `EvidencePage` |
471	| `POST /v1/memory/status` | `StatusQuery` | `MemoryStatus` |
472	
473	Use JSON and runtime validation. Reject unknown fields, malformed unions, invalid times, non-finite vectors, mismatched vector spaces, duplicate operations on one source/contribution, and invalid budgets. Do not silently coerce identifiers or remove unsupported fields. Compile trusted server-owned schemas; never compile a schema supplied by a caller. [S2]
474	
475	Return `200` after a successful canonical write even when `retrievalReady` is false; the receipt states the distinction. Use the following domain-error body:
476	
477	```json
478	{ "error": { "code": "VERSION_CONFLICT", "message": "Expected revision does not match.", "requestId": "opaque-id" } }
479	```
480	
481	Map `INVALID_INPUT` to `400`; `ACCESS_DENIED` to `403`; permitted `NOT_FOUND` to `404`; version/idempotency/stale-support conflicts to `409`; `INDEX_NOT_READY` to `409`; unavailable retained views to `410`; and request/graph budget failures to `422` (oversized HTTP envelopes may use `413`). Missing authentication is `401`. Rate limits, service failure, and temporary unavailability remain transport errors (`429`, `500`, `503`), not invented members of the contract's domain-error union. The SDK must distinguish transport failure from a typed memory-domain failure.
482	
483	Do not disclose existence, head values, policy identities, counts, or dependency names for forbidden resources in errors. Check authorization before giving conflict detail. Parameterize all SQL and never accept Cypher/SQL execution through the API.
484	
485	### Self-contained identity and policies
486	
487	Start with local opaque API keys, not a mandatory identity-provider connection. `BUSINESS_ID` is fixed at first initialization and persisted; starting an existing volume with a different business ID fails. Jive provisions one principal/key per trust scope rather than giving every workflow an administrative key.
488	
489	`BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN` authorizes administration on first setup and subsequent authenticated control calls; it is not a normal agent credential. Require a high-entropy secret, keep it out of logs and image layers, and support rotation. Principal keys are generated from cryptographically secure random bytes and stored only as hashes. The API resolves the key to a business-bound principal and current grants on each request. Revoked keys stop authorizing new requests immediately at the next authorization point.
490	
491	Implement these Jive-controlled routes on the same port, separately authorized from memory access:
492	
493	- `PUT /v1/admin/principals/{id}`: create/disable a principal and set allowed adapter/contribution namespaces; version-check edits.
494	- `POST /v1/admin/principals/{id}/keys`: issue a key once; `DELETE .../keys/{keyId}` revokes it.
495	- `PUT /v1/admin/policies/{id}`: versioned policy with explicit reader and writer principal IDs. Readers/writers are separate; a writer also needs read permission for evidence it uses.
496	- `PUT /v1/admin/source-bindings/{sourceId}`: reserve an allowed policy and project labels for a source. A normal `SourceChange` must match an authorized binding; it cannot downgrade a source's policy.
497	
498	For a demo, bootstrap these through a documented `memory-admin seed-demo` command bundled in the same image. No Jive backend, external account, or connector should be required to run the fixtures. Production Jive can call the same control routes. Groups and signed-token integration may be added later without altering the knowledge contract.
499	
500	A writer can replace/retract only its assigned contribution namespace or one explicitly delegated by the control plane. Validate `producer.adapter` and permitted provenance bases against its registration. A caller cannot gain trust by putting `compiler-derived` in JSON.
501	
502	Every source-dependent result requires current access to all transitive leaf sources. This includes entity aliases, summaries, graph intermediate edges, evidence, history, invalidations, and search candidates. System invalidation still traverses all affected contributions in the business; any counts or details returned to the initiating writer must be restricted to what that writer can read. Reauthorization of an idempotent receipt must also protect those counts.
503	
504	For database defense in depth, enable business row-level security and use non-owner application roles without `BYPASSRLS`. Source-level logic is an additional check, not replaced by business isolation. Migration and maintenance roles are separate; never expose their credentials to the HTTP application. PostgreSQL documents the owner/superuser bypass cases. [S5]
505	
506	The consistency point for reads is the start of their bounded repeatable-read database transaction, after credential resolution. Permission changes completed before that point must apply; an already-running response may finish under its prior policy snapshot. State this explicitly rather than claiming to retract bytes already delivered. [S10]
507	
508	## 9. Database model
509	
510	All business-owned keys, joins, indexes, and foreign keys include `business_id`, even when the default instance contains one business. Store sequence numbers as PostgreSQL `bigint`; keep them internal so JavaScript number precision is not a hidden API dependency. Public IDs are opaque strings.
511	
512	| Table(s) | Key and required data |
513	|---|---|
514	| `instance_state`, `business_state` | Instance/business identity, schema version, canonical sequence, readable sequence, policy epoch, active index generation, ordered record time |
515	| `writes` | `(business_id, principal_id, idempotency_key)` unique; canonical batch hash, write/snapshot IDs, sequence, recorded time, original receipt and exposure requirements |
516	| `snapshots` | Snapshot ID, business, sequence, recorded time, index generation, publication status, retention state |
517	| `sources` | Stable source ID, type, current head, active/tombstoned flag, current binding/policy, project membership |
518	| `source_head_history` | Source ID/head/type/state/project labels with `[from_seq,to_seq)` intervals |
519	| `evidence_versions` | `(source_id,item_id,version)` within business; immutable JSON/text or blob ID, media type, locator, URL, occurrence time, payload hash |
520	| `evidence_membership` | Which evidence version belongs to a source item over each knowledge-sequence interval |
521	| `contributions` | Stable contribution ID, last version/head, registered writer namespace |
522	| `contribution_versions` | Immutable full `Contribution` payload/hash, producer/basis, created sequence |
523	| `contribution_state_history` | Current/stale/retracted state of a contribution version over sequence intervals |
524	| `entity_keys` | Stable internal entity keys only; no globally readable merged names |
525	| `entity_descriptions` | Entity fields from a particular contribution version, never a permission-free canonical description |
526	| `assertions` | Contribution version and assertion-local ID; subject/predicate; object kind/entity/value; stance; valid-time bounds |
527	| `summaries`, `summary_subjects` | Contribution version, summary-local ID/text, referenced entity IDs |
528	| `evidence_dependencies` | Contribution version -> exact evidence version; reverse index required |
529	| `contribution_dependencies` | Dependent contribution version -> supporting contribution version; reverse index required |
530	| `contribution_sources` | Deduplicated set of transitive leaf source IDs per contribution version, for current-policy authorization |
531	| `invalidations` | Affected contribution/version, triggering support, reason, invalidation sequence; stable paging key |
532	| `search_units` | Immutable unit ID, contribution version, renderer generation, prepared text, lexical `tsvector`, required-source cohort |
533	| `search_vectors` | Unit ID + embedding generation, vector, source cohort; no mixed vector spaces |
534	| `index_jobs`, `index_publications` | Lease, attempt count, retry time, unit/generation identity, completion/error, per-snapshot remaining work |
535	| `principals`, `principal_keys`, `policies`, `source_bindings` | Local control registry, versioned edits, key hashes, adapter/write scopes and grants |
536	| `blob_objects` | Business/owner, immutable object path, byte length, checksum, completed/staged status and reachability |
537	| `audit_events`, `maintenance_state` | Safe operational events, maintenance gates, backup/purge records |
538	
539	Use separate columns for an entity object and a JSON literal plus an `object_kind` discriminator; a literal JSON `null` is valid and must not be confused with “missing object.” Assertion IDs and summary IDs are local to their contribution version. Add foreign keys, interval checks, unique active-head constraints, and supporting indexes in SQL migrations.
540	
541	Required indexes include:
542	
543	- `(business_id, subject, predicate)` and `(business_id, object_entity, predicate)` for adjacency in each direction.
544	- Both directions of each dependency table; `(business_id, source_id, contribution_id, version)` for inherited authorization lookup.
545	- Source/item/head/version and contribution/head/version lookups; sequence interval access paths for history.
546	- GIN over prepared lexical text; vector search strategy described in section 12. GIN is a documented PostgreSQL full-text index option. [S6]
547	
548	An entity description from a private source must never be copied into an unrestricted shared entity row. If two sources name the same entity differently, preserve their contributed descriptions. If two IDs might refer to the same entity, an adapter may submit an evidence-backed identity relationship; the database does not merge them by display name.
549	
550	### History without copying the graph
551	
552	A write gets one business sequence. It closes/open membership and state intervals; immutable payloads stay intact. The snapshot's source-head map is reconstructed from history. Unchanged items and contributions keep their versions across unrelated source changes.
553	
554	Repository branches are separate sources. Exact package versions and cross-repository symbol identities come from code adapters; a memory snapshot does not prove that all repositories are part of a coordinated deployed release. A release manifest can itself be evidence that relates the appropriate versions.
555	
556	## 10. `apply`: atomic write algorithm
557	
558	Use one checked-out `pg` client and one canonical transaction. Initially serialize canonical writes within the business using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on `business_state`. This is a deliberate correctness-first throughput tradeoff. Do not perform model encoding, filesystem uploads, or external calls while holding the write lock. [S3, S10]
559	
560	1. Authenticate and validate shape/size. Resolve allowed source bindings and write namespaces. Stage immutable large inputs and verify referenced blobs before transaction promotion.
561	2. Acquire the business lock. Check the principal-scoped idempotency record. Identical authorized replays return the original receipt; different payloads fail.
562	3. Check expected source and contribution heads against the locked canonical state. Reject duplicate operations for one head and attempts to mutate an immutable version.
563	4. Build the post-batch source state. Change only mentioned items; tombstones remove all current membership of that source. Updating only a source head does not change unchanged evidence versions.
564	5. Seed invalidation with every removed/replaced current evidence version and every replaced/retracted current contribution version. Traverse the reverse dependency graph to obtain all dependent contribution versions.
565	6. Mark affected surviving heads stale in the same transaction, close prior state intervals, and persist invalidation records. The logical closure is global within the business, not limited by what the initiating writer can see.
566	7. Validate new contributions in dependency order against the post-batch state. All dependencies must exist, belong to this business, be current at the required exact version, and terminate in evidence. Reject cycles and stale support. New supports in the same batch are allowed.
567	8. Insert immutable contribution payloads, contributed graph records, dependency edges, leaf-source sets, lexical search units, and index jobs. A same-batch replacement supported by the new evidence can become current immediately.
568	9. Allocate the snapshot sequence, ordered knowledge timestamp, publication bookkeeping, and receipt. Persist only authorized invalidation counts in the receipt. Commit and then return it.
569	
570	For the v0.1 invalidation reason enum, replacement/removal of an evidence item maps to `evidence-changed`/`evidence-removed`; replacement or retraction of a contribution support maps to `support-retracted`. The exact `changedSupport` identifies the affected version.
571	
572	Replacing a contribution invalidates consumers of its old version even when its text appears similar. A changed identity description does not automatically invalidate every incoming business edge; only explicit support dependencies do. Retracting one source's claim does not delete another source's independent claim or a still-supported entity.
573	
574	Use indexed reverse-dependency queries, not a scan of the whole graph. PostgreSQL's recursive queries can implement a closure; an iterative temporary frontier table can be used where it gives better bounds and instrumentation. [S4]
575	
576	**High-fanout correctness:** when a write exceeds a configured invalidation or transaction budget, abort the entire write. Never accept the source change and promise to invalidate it later. Large imports can stage rows and promote them with a longer controlled transaction; readers must not see a partly applied source revision. Report this limit and benchmark it. If common updates cannot fit, treat that as a design-gate failure requiring a new atomic invalidation strategy, not a reason to disable the check.
577	
578	Public writes have configurable payload limits. Provide a same-image administrative bulk-import command using the same validator and transaction/promotion code for large initial datasets. It may stream into private staging tables. It must not bypass permissions or invent intermediate source heads solely to make a large update look complete.
579	
580	## 11. Indexing and snapshot publication
581	
582	The internal indexer leases persisted jobs with short database transactions, computes outside them, and publishes results idempotently by immutable unit ID and generation. PostgreSQL's `SKIP LOCKED` supports the proposed queue-claiming pattern. It is used only for this maintenance work, not for consistent user reads. [S11]
583	
584	A process crash loses a lease, not a write. Expired leases are reclaimable. A job that repeatedly fails must remain operationally visible; it must not be marked complete to let the publication watermark advance.
585	
586	### Search units and embeddings
587	
588	Render searchable text from contributed names/aliases, literal assertions, and summaries. Code references and structural edges use adjacency indexes; do not generate one embedding per reference edge. When splitting text into embedding units, preserve the mapping back to whole immutable contributions.
589	
590	Search rendering may use a contribution's own content and declared supports only. Pulling a name or description from an unrelated record creates an undeclared freshness/permission dependency and is forbidden.
591	
592	The initial embedding space uses the selected E5 model's required query/passage formatting, pooling, normalization, dimensions, and input limits. Verify these against its model card and tokenizer assets. Record the exact ONNX/model revision, tokenizer revision, renderer/chunker version, and vector dimension in an `embedding-space.json` manifest. [S8]
593	
594	Use bounded overlapping passage chunks within the model's input limit. Overlong queries are rejected, not silently truncated. Keep the API's local query encoder out of the HTTP event loop's synchronous work; use an internal worker thread or process. Bound indexer batches and CPU threads so bulk ingestion does not starve reads.
595	
596	Model/tokenizer assets are fetched and verified **during image construction**, pinned to immutable revisions and checksums, and shipped in the final image. Disable runtime download fallbacks and telemetry. Startup and queries must pass tests with outbound traffic denied. A missing model is a readiness failure, not permission to contact a hosted inference service.
597	
598	### Publication
599	
600	Canonical graph/lexical rows are written transactionally; required embeddings can complete later. Each snapshot has a set of required projection work for the active generation. Advance the readable sequence only over a contiguous run of finished snapshots, preserving explicit readiness for retained historical snapshots.
601	
602	This intentionally allows index work at an earlier snapshot to delay later publication. Record that head-of-line risk in metrics; do not claim later snapshots are fully ready while skipped required history is missing. Operators can repair/retry or explicitly retire unavailable history through maintenance; the service cannot silently falsify it.
603	
604	A new embedding model builds a new generation beside the old one. Switch only after coverage is complete for the supported views. Never compare vectors from different generations/spaces. Validate caller-supplied vector length, finite elements, and `space` against the selected view's generation.
605	
606	## 12. `retrieve`: query execution and safety
607	
608	### 12.1 Establish eligible knowledge
609	
610	Authenticate, encode a text query when needed, then open a bounded repeatable-read database transaction for view and policy resolution. Load current grants, canonical state, selected readable snapshot, and active generation together. Evaluate membership/state at the requested view and apply the latest-view safety mask from section 7. Indexes cannot override canonical invalidation or revocation.
611	
612	Build an eligible contribution relation before user-visible ranking or traversal. It applies business, all supporting-source permissions, snapshot visibility, stale/valid-time rules, and source/project relevance scope. Entity descriptors have the same eligibility as their owning contributions.
613	
614	### 12.2 Text retrieval
615	
616	Retrieve lexical candidates from prepared text and semantic candidates from stored embeddings; fuse authorized ranks deterministically, for example using `1 / (60 + rank)` per retrieval channel as an initial service-defined rule. Deduplicate by contribution version. Those coefficients are tuning choices to evaluate, not a claim of optimality.
617	
618	Use selected candidates to seed a small adjacency expansion through authorized assertions and summaries. The v1 text path expands asserted relationships; proposed/negated statements can be retrieved as evidence-bearing text, but are not interpreted as affirmative connectivity for inferred expansion. Explicit graph queries preserve and return their stance.
619	
620	No generative query planner, LLM reranker, source checkout, connector access, or on-demand knowledge builder belongs in this path. A consumer that needs a broader investigation must ask Jive to run it separately.
621	
622	### 12.3 Vector authorization and scale
623	
624	Implement an **exact-distance search over an authorized materialized set** as the correctness/recall reference. It may not meet the latency goal at full scale; report that rather than calling it production-fast.
625	
626	The production optimization to test is HNSW partitions/cohorts keyed by business and the complete required-source set, so a query only searches cohorts whose every source is authorized. Cache cohort eligibility only with the principal and current policy epoch. Recheck canonical time/state/scope filters on candidates before assembling context. Where cohorts are too numerous or permissions are highly fragmented, retain the exact path and report the latency impact.
627	
628	The physical ANN search may touch time-ineligible vectors within an otherwise authorized cohort, so measure historical/current recall separately. Do not search a shared cross-permission ANN index and treat output filtering as equivalent to permission-safe candidate selection. pgvector documents post-index filtering and cross-tenant recall interference; its approximate indexes trade recall for speed. [S7]
629	
630	An optimized path is accepted only against exact permitted top-k results and the workload in section 17. If cohort fragmentation makes the approach too slow, isolate that finding and propose an alternative within the single-image boundary. Do not hide it behind a vendor benchmark.
631	
632	### 12.4 Typed graph retrieval
633	
634	Translate `startEntityIds` and `steps` into parameterized adjacency operations. Track the frontier per step, authorize every assertion and descriptor, and deduplicate by entity/step plus returned contribution identity. Do not block legitimate revisits at another step merely because a business graph is cyclic.
635	
636	Require `steps.length <= maxHops`; reject unbounded wildcard predicates. Use indexes in both directions. Implement internal maximums for edges examined, frontier width, support expansions, execution time, and output bytes in addition to the public budgets. `LIMIT` on the final response is not a bound on the work needed to discover it.
637	
638	A path may traverse only authorized contributions; reaching an accessible endpoint through a forbidden intermediate edge is not allowed. A known entity ID alone must not reveal restricted aliases or descriptions.
639	
640	### 12.5 Context assembly
641	
642	Select whole contribution versions, then attach exact leaf evidence references and bounded excerpts from stored text. Traverse provenance separately under its own work/citation budget. If a contribution's evidence closure cannot fit the permitted response, omit it rather than silently presenting it as fully cited. Blob-only evidence returns its reference/locator; do not fabricate a text excerpt from binary bytes.
643	
644	`sourceHeads` contains the authorized sources relevant to returned knowledge and its evidence. `status` can page all permitted sources; retrieval does not enumerate the entire business for every question. Gap messages and timing/audit payloads must not name or count inaccessible knowledge.
645	
646	Do not introduce an assembled-context cache in the first release. A future cache needs principal/scope, policy epoch, snapshot, canonical validity epoch, query, budget, and index generation, plus revocation tests.
647	
648	## 13. Evidence and status implementations
649	
650	### Immutable evidence transport
651	
652	Small text is stored directly in PostgreSQL. Large text/binary evidence uses `payload.blobId`. Build a separate `POST /v1/evidence/blobs` streaming upload on the same port; it returns an opaque blob ID, size, and SHA-256 checksum. A blob belongs to the authenticated business/principal until evidence references bind it to source policies.
653	
654	Upload into a private staging path. Bound size, compute/verify checksums, fsync completed data, atomically rename to a generated immutable path, and make the parent directory durable before a canonical transaction can reference it. Paths never come from user filenames or `sourceUrl`. Validate ownership/completion in `apply`.
655	
656	This avoids pretending filesystem and SQL writes share a transaction: completed bytes precede the database reference; unreferenced uploads may later be garbage-collected after a safety period. A crash may leave an orphan, but must not leave a committed reference to incomplete bytes.
657	
658	`readEvidence` checks current source access for each exact version, including historical evidence, and returns the original stored item. Its signed cursor is bound to business, principal, request refs, ordering, and budget, with an expiration. Recheck permissions on every page.
659	
660	`GET /v1/evidence/blobs/{blobId}` streams bytes only after authorizing a referring evidence item (or the staged object's authorized uploader). An opaque ID is not a bearer credential. Apply byte/range limits and avoid redirecting to an unprotected file URL. No stored URL is fetched server-side.
661	
662	### Status
663	
664	`status` resolves canonical permitted source heads, requested write publication, and current stale invalidations. Page source/invalidations collections deterministically with one signed cursor containing a stable canonical cutoff and individual table positions. Recheck current permission and whether an invalidation is still relevant; filter resolved entries without exposing forbidden counts.
665	
666	After pagination begins, new invalidations beyond that cutoff appear in a subsequent fresh scan. Jive owns scan cursors/retry scheduling, not this service. Empty stores have an initial readable snapshot so `latestReadableSnapshotId` is defined.

786	## 15. Single-image build and lifecycle specification
787	
788	### Image contents
789	
790	Produce a multi-stage Docker build with a **single final runtime image** containing PostgreSQL 18, pgvector, Node.js 24, compiled application/SDK support files, the indexer, pinned local model/tokenizer assets, Tini, migration scripts, and administrative maintenance commands. Build stages are not deployed services.
791	
792	A concrete database base to verify and pin is `pgvector/pgvector:0.8.7-pg18-bookworm`, which the project documents. Resolve a content digest and lock all Node/npm/model inputs in the implementation rather than leaving mutable production tags. Build for `linux/amd64`; add an arm64 manifest only after native-extension and model-runtime tests pass. [S7]
793	
794	The image must not download packages or model files at startup. Do not include a registry credential, business API key, database data directory, or fixture business data in image layers.
795	
796	### Process lifecycle
797	
798	Use Tini as PID 1 to handle child reaping and forward termination to an image-local coordinator. Tini is not the application supervisor; implement and test start/failure/stop ordering in the coordinator. [S13]
799	
800	Startup:
801	
802	1. Validate required configuration and writable data storage; claim an instance lock so a second live container cannot use the same directory.
803	2. On an empty volume, initialize subdirectories and protected instance metadata. Do not silently initialize over an invalid or newer-version database.
804	3. Start PostgreSQL as a non-root database user. Set `listen_addresses=''`; use a private Unix-domain socket and explicit local authentication. No database TCP port is exposed. PostgreSQL documents Unix-socket-only operation. [S14]
805	4. Bootstrap separate database owner/migration, application, and maintenance roles. The application does not hold superuser credentials. Permission initialization may require a short privileged entrypoint on a fresh mounted volume; API, indexer, and PostgreSQL run as non-root users. Support a pre-owned volume mode without a privileged bootstrap.
806	5. Run versioned migrations under an exclusive migration lock. Refuse incompatible schema/database major versions with an actionable error.
807	6. Start the API and internal indexer, load the bundled encoder, and run a small model self-check. Readiness turns healthy only after mandatory components are available.
808	
809	On API, indexer, or PostgreSQL fatal process failure, withdraw readiness and terminate the appliance with a nonzero exit after controlled cleanup. The host may restart the whole container. Do not leave a permanently “healthy” API with a dead publication worker. Transient index jobs retry; a fatal indexer process is a lifecycle event.
810	
811	On `SIGTERM`, stop accepting writes, stop leasing new index work, drain bounded requests, close client pools, stop the indexer, and shut PostgreSQL down in order using its control tools. Tini must forward to the coordinator rather than indiscriminately kill all children before this ordering. Test forced host termination and WAL recovery as well as graceful exit.
812	
813	Keep durability protections enabled; never turn off fsync or synchronous commit to win a latency benchmark. Store PostgreSQL files/WAL and evidence on `/data`, not the container's disposable writable layer. A single image update must never auto-upgrade a PostgreSQL major version against an incompatible data directory.
814	
815	### Public host contract
816	
817	| Configuration | Meaning |
818	|---|---|
819	| `PORT=8080` | HTTP bind port; bind on `0.0.0.0` |
820	| `DATA_DIR=/data` | Writable durable data mount |
821	| `BUSINESS_ID` | Required server-side business identity; immutable for that volume |
822	| `BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN` | Required high-entropy administrator credential or supported secret-file equivalent |
823	| `LOG_LEVEL=info` | Structured logging level, with content/secret redaction |
824	| `INDEX_CONCURRENCY=1` | Initial background-maintenance concurrency cap |
825	| Resource/budget settings | Document safe bounds for DB pools, encoder threads, batch sizes, query time, disk use, and retention |
826	
827	Implement `GET /health/live` and `GET /health/ready` on the same port. Health responses reveal component state only, not business data. An unpublished new snapshot does not make the entire service unavailable if previously published views remain valid. Administrative diagnostics expose job errors/backlogs under separate authorization.
828	
829	Use generic HTTP/TLS handling: local HTTP is acceptable for development; production must use transport encryption supplied by the host ingress or configured service TLS. There is no dependency on a particular proxy product or hosting platform.

857	### Capacity and operational limits
858	
859	One active writer instance owns the database/filesystem. This design supports many concurrent API clients and workflows, not multiple independent containers writing the same volume. Use vertical scaling and measured resource limits for this release. Increasing replica count is not a supported high-availability mechanism.
860	
861	An application/database upgrade may require a restart window. A volume protects against container replacement, not against losing the underlying storage. Set maintenance windows and backup policy at the operator/Jive layer. These are consequences of the selected single-node design, not rules from a hosting vendor.
862	
863	## 16. Backup, retention, deletion, and observability
864	
865	Ship same-image `memory-admin` commands for initialization checks, import, backup, restore, and purge. They are maintenance operations, not extra workflow engines or agent memory methods.
866	
867	For the first correct backup implementation, acquire a maintenance gate, pause canonical writes/blob garbage collection/index publication, drain active mutations, and create a PostgreSQL logical dump plus a manifest and exact copies of the evidence blobs referenced by that dump. PostgreSQL documents the logical-dump mechanism; coherence with external evidence files is additional service work. [S15]
868	
869	Include schema/index/model versions, roles/control registry needed for restore, checksum manifests, source-head snapshot, and recovery instructions. Restore into a fresh directory and verify references, permissions, checksums, and a golden query. Do not copy live PostgreSQL files as though they were ordinary documents. Keep the first backup mechanism conservative; online hot-backup optimizations require a separate consistency proof.
870	
871	A backup left on the same volume is not independent disaster recovery. Jive/operators export the backup off-host through their chosen mechanisms. No external backup provider is mandatory for normal service operation, but independent backup storage is an operational responsibility.
872	
873	Source tombstones retain history and are **not** hard deletion. Before production use, implement an administrator-only purge that removes targeted evidence and all derived contribution versions depending on it, their index units/vectors, now-unreferenced blobs, and any cached/temporary artifacts. Recompute reachability so another source's independent support is not destroyed. Mark historical snapshots requiring purged records unavailable rather than pretending to reproduce them. Coordinate purge with backups and document the backup-expiration policy; already exported copies cannot be instantly recalled by this service.
874	
875	Logs contain request IDs, permitted identifiers, timing, row/job counts, and safe failure codes—not source text, prompts, credentials, vectors, or private aliases. Metrics include canonical/readable lag, write-lock duration, invalidation fanout, query phases, exact/ANN recall, index attempts, encoder memory, database resource use, volume free space, and backup age. Never expose business-level diagnostics through public health routes.
876	
877	Data remains untrusted input. Do not execute uploaded code, follow embedded URLs, interpret source text as instructions, or grant capabilities based on facts in the graph. Returned evidence is labeled data for the consuming agent; the memory service is not a prompt-injection filter or execution sandbox.
878	
879	## 17. Acceptance tests and performance gates
880	
881	Every mandatory test must be executable from the implementation repository. Tests exercise the published Docker image as one container, not a mock database that bypasses the packaged topology.
882	
883	| Test | Required result |
884	|---|---|
885	| A1: shared workflows | Two permitted principals retrieve shared knowledge without copying it into separate agent histories. |
886	| A2: isolated businesses | Instances/volumes for two businesses cannot access each other's records, tokens, cursors, or blobs. Wrong volume identity fails startup. |
887	| A3: generic input | Meeting, CRM/operations, and compiler-derived fixtures use the same four methods; provenance survives round-trips. |
888	| A4: idempotency/CAS | Duplicate concurrent batches yield one effect/original receipt; conflicting payloads/heads are rejected. |
889	| A5: item-granular updates | A source head advance with unchanged evidence invalidates nothing; changed/removed support invalidates exactly its declared transitive dependents. |
890	| A6: independent support | Retraction of one contribution preserves another source's independent support and valid entity descriptions. |
891	| A7: delayed extraction | A contribution based on superseded support is rejected, including races with an incoming evidence change. |
892	| A8: support graph | Same-batch dependencies work; cycles, wrong-business references, and missing supports fail atomically. |
893	| A9: history | Different source heads coexist in one snapshot; knowledge time and world-validity time behave as specified. |
894	| A10: index lag | Pause the indexer, commit a correction, and verify no current read presents the old claim as current; exact unready snapshots fail explicitly. |
895	| A11: permission closure | Revocation prevents lexical/vector retrieval, paths through intermediate edges, aliases, evidence, history, gaps, counts, and cursor replays from leaking restricted material. |
896	| A12: write authorization | A workflow cannot edit another producer's namespace, claim an unregistered provenance basis, or downgrade a source policy. |
897	| A13: output/work budgets | High-degree graphs, long provenance chains, mixed-validity contributions, and oversized evidence have explicit bounded behavior. |
898	| A14: disconnected reads | Disable connector/source access and outbound networking; prepared text and graph queries still work, including local encoding. |
899	| A15: single-container restart | Stop/remove the container, start the same image with the same volume, and recover evidence, graph, jobs, policy state, and queries. |
900	| A16: failure recovery | Kill API/indexer/database processes and the entire container during writes/indexing/uploads. Recover without half-applied revisions or missing committed blobs. |
901	| A17: backup/restore/purge | Restore database and evidence together to a fresh volume; purge originals and derivatives without deleting independent support. |
902	| A18: packaged isolation | No exposed PostgreSQL TCP listener, no required external connection, no source execution, no default plaintext secrets. |
903	| A19: database upgrades | Incompatible data/schema versions refuse startup without changing data; documented upgrade/rollback tests pass. |
904	| A20: high-fanout/import | Large imports and invalidations either commit coherently or fail atomically; normal reads are measured during these operations. |

906	### Benchmark specification
907	
908	The target is **p95 below 200 ms for warm storage retrieval**, not end-to-end answer generation. Report query embedding time, HTTP transport, and total response time separately and together. This is an unverified acceptance target; it is not a guarantee for arbitrary questions or hardware.
909	
910	Use two fixtures. A small fixture makes tests fast. The scale fixture represents approximately 200 repositories plus meeting/CRM/operations sources, 2 million entities, 10 million assertions, 1 million contributions, and 500,000 prepared search units. These are proposed test inputs, not a claim of supported capacity or a sizing estimate for every business.
911	
912	Measure on declared CPU/RAM/storage and container limits; propose a starting scale-test machine of 16 vCPU, 64 GiB RAM, and SSD storage sized after measuring the generated fixture. This is a test setup, not the application's minimum resource requirement. Measure a small deployment separately rather than extrapolating.
913	
914	Include 20 reads/second with concurrent writes, mixed 0–3-hop graph queries, text queries with 4,000-token/30-contribution output budgets, warm/cold encoder conditions, skewed degree distributions, historical reads, sparse matches, and multiple permission-fragmentation levels. Run long enough to show steady-state indexing and storage growth.
915	
916	Record p50/p95/p99, peak memory, query plan/rows examined, publication lag, invalidation transaction duration, lock contention, index build cost, disk footprint, and recovery time. Compare approximate search to exact authorized top-20 results; an initial gate is at least 0.95 recall@20 for approximate versus exact vector ranking, measured separately by scope/history cohort. Also maintain human-reviewed expected-evidence sets for at least 50 representative questions: exact vector recall alone does not prove that business context is relevant or correct.
917	
918	Fail security tests on any unauthorized content; average recall or good latency cannot compensate. Report benchmark failures with the responsible phase, not as a vague “scalability issue.” Do not silently relax authorization, invalidation, provenance, or output completeness to meet 200 ms.
