# Jive Knowledge Graph — Design

**Status:** Draft for review · **Date:** 2026-10-10 · **Author:** Alex Leung (with Claude)
**Supersedes:** `jive-memory-agent-handoff.md` (Codex, rev 0.2)

---

## 1. What we are building

Every Jive project gets one **brain**: a shared, durable body of knowledge that any agent working on that project can read and write. The ideal reader is a "super worker" who is simultaneously staff engineer, designer, TPM, and CEO, and therefore needs accurate knowledge of everything: how the code works, how the business works, who owns what, what was decided, what was promised, and what people intend to build.

Examples of projects and the knowledge their brains accumulate:

| Project | Knowledge comes from | Example facts |
|---|---|---|
| DAT (employer) | Code, Confluence, meetings, Slack, agent work | "Rate service X computes lane rates via Y", "Team Z owns X", "We committed to customer A by Oct 23" |
| Game decompilation (personal) | Binary, decompiled C, subagent results | "Function 0x4012F0 matches byte for byte", "Struct `Player` is 0x48 bytes" |

The Knowledge Graph is a **Jive interface**, in the same way that Message Board (Slack, Discord) and Task Board (Linear, Jira) are interfaces. Implementations are Convex components that act as thin adapters and call an external backend over HTTP. This document specifies the interface and recommends the backend.

**Immediate use:** before Jive launches, Alex uses the brain standalone. Claude reads DAT code and documents and writes into it, and agents get skills for querying it. Automated workflows (on commit, after meetings) come later and later move into Jive.

## 2. Requirements

What each requirement is, and why it exists:

| # | Requirement | Why |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | **One brain per project, domain-neutral.** Code and business knowledge live together and cross-link. | The super worker's questions span both ("which customer commitments depend on this service?"). |
| R2 | **Every fact records its evidence and how it was derived** (compiler, imported, human, model). | Accuracy. Many agents write over time and some will be wrong. A claim without a source can't be checked or challenged. |
| R3 | **Facts whose evidence has changed are detectable as possibly stale.** Agents and workflows do the fixing; the brain only points. | "Improve the graph on commit" requires knowing what the commit invalidated. |
| R4 | **Conflicting claims coexist with their evidence.** Nothing is overwritten by whoever wrote last. | A Slack message can't override what the code does. A reply of "you're wrong, here's the code reference" must win on evidence, not recency. |
| R5 | **Code structure is compiler-exact**, not LLM-guessed. | "A calls B" is either true or false, and a compiler knows which. |
| R6 | **Writers are attributed, and one writer can't silently destroy another's facts.** Bad writes can be rolled back by writer. | A misbehaving workflow should be containable. |
| R7 | **The interface is backend-agnostic**, so the Jive adapter stays thin. | Same pattern as other Jive interfaces. The backend can be swapped as needs grow. |
| R8 | **Usable this week.** | Alex needs to start building the DAT corpus now. |

### Claim kinds (nuance behind R4)

Claims about a system fall into three kinds, and which evidence is authoritative depends on the kind:

| Kind | Example | Authoritative evidence |
|---|---|---|
| `current` | "Retries use a fixed 5s delay" | Code and compiler output. Runtime data. |
| `intended` | "Retries should back off exponentially" | Design docs, ADRs, decisions by owners |
| `aspiration` | "We want a self-serve pricing API in 2027" | Roadmaps, strategy docs, leadership statements |

Code is authoritative on **what the system does**, not on **what it should do**. A Slack message saying "the retry logic is wrong" can't be rebutted by the code, because the code is the thing in dispute.

**Decision:** `kind` is an **optional** field. Writers set it when it's clear. Readers otherwise infer it from the source type: compiler output → `current`, design doc → `intended`, roadmap → `aspiration`. We'll formalize it further only if drift questions ("where does reality diverge from intent?") turn out to be common.

### Explicit non-goals

- **Read permissions.** Everything in a project's brain is visible to every agent and person using that project. In most companies, docs and code are broadly readable, so read restriction is the rare exception. The project boundary is the only wall.
- **Automatic truth adjudication.** The brain ranks claims by evidence but doesn't declare winners.
- **Automatic re-extraction.** The brain never calls an LLM, crawls a source, or fixes a fact by itself.
- **Copying code structure into the brain.** See §4.3.
- **The heavy machinery of the Codex design:** transitive atomic invalidation, snapshot publication, a three-clock temporal model, per-source ACLs, and one-container Postgres packaging. Each one solved a requirement we don't have.

## 3. Options considered

### 3.1 Candidates

**A. Graphiti** (open source, from Zep). A Python framework for temporal knowledge graphs. Per its README, it requires Neo4j, FalkorDB, or Neptune, plus an LLM and embedding API. It ingests text "episodes" and uses an LLM to extract entities and edges. It has an MCP server and a REST service, and it invalidates contradicted facts automatically while keeping their history.

**B. Zep.** The managed version of the Graphiti engine, with SLAs and a proprietary graph store.

**C. Brain-as-repo.** Knowledge is stored as structured text files in a git repository. Claude reads and writes it directly now, and a thin service exposes it through the interface later. Sourcegraph can optionally index it alongside the real code repos.

**D. Custom service.** A purpose-built database service, essentially a simplified Codex design.

### 3.2 Evaluation

| Requirement | A. Graphiti | B. Zep | C. Brain-as-repo | D. Custom |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1 domain-neutral, cross-linked | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| R2 evidence per fact | Partial: facts trace to episodes, not to exact quotes/versions you choose | Partial (same) | **Yes**: explicit source fields, plus git author, time, and message | Yes |
| R3 stale detection | Its own temporal invalidation, not source-version-based | Same | **Yes**: compare recorded source versions to current ones (§5) | Yes |
| R4 evidence-weighted conflicts | **Conflict:** it auto-invalidates contradicted facts. Whether that's recency- or LLM-driven needs verifying, but it isn't evidence-ranked. | Same | **Yes**: claims coexist, and rebuttals cite evidence | Yes |
| R5 compiler-exact code | No: LLM extraction | No | **Yes**, by linking to SCIP symbols (§4.3) | Yes |
| R6 writer attribution and rollback | Limited | Limited | **Yes**: one commit per write, and `git revert` by writer | Yes, but must be built |
| R7 behind a thin adapter | Yes (REST) | Yes (API) | Yes, once the service exists (Phase 1) | Yes |
| R8 usable this week | Yes, about an hour (estimate) | Yes, but it's a paid account | **Yes, today** | **No**: weeks |
| Write control | Low: an LLM decides what's stored | Low | **Full**: the writer writes exactly the fact | Full |
| Cost per write | One LLM call | Included in plan | Free | Free |
| Multi-hop graph queries | Strong | Strong | **Weak** until Phase 2's derived index | Strong |
| Many concurrent writers | Good | Good | **Merge friction** until Phase 1 serializes writes | Good |

### 3.3 Recommendation: C (brain-as-repo), behind the Jive interface from day one

The deciding factors:

1. **R4 rules out A and B as the system of record.** Their core feature, automatic contradiction invalidation, is the opposite of evidence-weighted coexistence. A Slack message could retire a code-backed fact.
2. **R2 and R5 favor exact writes over LLM extraction.** The brain's value is accuracy. Running every write through another model's interpretation adds an unaccountable error source.
3. **Git already provides most of what the Codex design built by hand:** an immutable history, attribution, diffs, review, time travel, and revert.
4. **It's usable today, and it doesn't lock us in.** The interface (§6) hides the repo. If scale or graph-query needs outgrow it, Phase 2 adds a derived database index that is rebuilt from the repo, and the repo stays the source of truth.

Accepted weaknesses: multi-hop queries are slow or manual until Phase 2, and concurrent writers need a single writer service (Phase 1). Both are cheap to fix and neither blocks the DAT corpus.

**When to revisit:** if Phase 2 triggers (§8) fire and a derived index isn't enough, re-evaluate D. Graphiti may still be useful as a **read-side helper** over the repo's content, but not as the system of record.

## 4. Data model

### 4.1 Entities

An entity is anything worth knowing about: a person, team, organization, service, repository, decision, commitment, process, concept, function, or struct. Each entity is one file.

```text
brain/
  entities/
    organization/acme.md
    person/alex-leung.md
    service/rate-engine.md
    decision/2026-09-rate-cache.md
  schema/            # predicate vocabulary + validator config
  BRAIN.md           # conventions for agents (the skill references this)
```

- **ID** is the file path without its extension, for example `service/rate-engine`. It's stable, readable, and greppable.
- **Types** are free strings with a recommended vocabulary in `schema/`. There's no hard-coded domain model.
- **Names aren't identities.** Two files that might be the same entity are linked with a `same-as` fact that carries evidence, never merged by name.

### 4.2 Facts

Facts live in the frontmatter of their **subject** entity's file. Prose below the frontmatter is a human- and LLM-readable summary, and it's also a fact (`predicate: summary`) with its own sources.

```markdown
---
id: service/rate-engine
type: service
name: Rate Engine
aliases: [rateengine, RE]
facts:
  - id: f-20261010-a1
    predicate: owned-by
    object: team/pricing-platform
    kind: current
    basis: imported
    writer: claude/dat-reader@1
    sources:
      - type: doc
        ref: confluence://PRICING/12345
        version: "v42"
        quote: "Pricing Platform team owns the Rate Engine."
  - id: f-20261010-a2
    predicate: retry-policy
    value: "fixed 5s delay, 3 attempts"
    kind: current
    basis: model-inferred
    writer: claude/dat-reader@1
    sources:
      - type: git
        repo: dat/rate-engine
        commit: 9f1c2ab
        path: src/client/retry.ts
        blob: 3b18e51
        lines: 12-30
  - id: f-20261010-a3
    predicate: retry-policy
    value: "exponential backoff"
    kind: intended
    basis: human-asserted
    writer: claude/dat-reader@1
    contradicts: [f-20261010-a2]
    sources:
      - type: message
        ref: slack://C0PRICING/1728400000.123
        version: original
        quote: "retry logic is wrong, it should back off exponentially"
---
The Rate Engine computes lane rates for ...
```

Field rules:

| Field | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | yes | Unique within the brain. Never reused. |
| `predicate` | yes | From the vocabulary in `schema/`. New predicates may be added, but the validator warns on unknown ones. |
| `object` / `value` | exactly one | `object` is an entity ID or code symbol (§4.3). `value` is a literal. |
| `kind` | no | `current`, `intended`, or `aspiration` (§2). |
| `basis` | yes | `compiler-derived`, `imported`, `human-asserted`, or `model-inferred`. This is a label, not proof. |
| `writer` | yes | Agent or workflow identity plus version. |
| `sources` | yes, ≥1 | Exact evidence (§5.1). A fact with no source is rejected. |
| `contradicts` | no | IDs of facts this one disputes. Both remain. |
| `status` | no | Absent means active. `retracted` (with `reason`) is set only by the fact's own writer or a human. |

Compiler-exact structure (definitions, references, call sites, types) **stays in the code and its SCIP index**. It is not copied into the brain, which avoids a whole class of staleness: structural facts can't go stale if they're never duplicated.

Structural questions ("who calls `computeRate`?") go to code intelligence, either Sourcegraph or a local SCIP index. | `message` | `ref` (platform, channel, timestamp) | `original` or the edit timestamp | Usually immutable. Check edits where the platform exposes them. |
| `meeting` | `ref` (transcript ID), segment | transcript revision | Compare the revision. |
| `artifact` | `ref` (build output, binary hash, test report) | content hash | Compare the hash. |
| `fact` | another fact's `id` | that fact's last-changed commit | Stale if the cited fact changed or was retracted. This is one hop only, not a transitive closure. |

The brain doesn't keep a stale flag that has to stay in sync. `brain stale [--scope <path|repo|source>]` computes stale facts on demand by running the checks in §5.1. Reads attach `freshness: fresh | stale | unverifiable` to each returned fact. After a commit lands, a workflow runs `brain stale --scope repo:<name>` and re-derives what it finds. That's the "improve the graph on commit" loop.

### 5.3 Contradictions

When a read returns a fact that has `contradicts` links in either direction, it returns the whole cluster. Ranking within the cluster follows the authority table in §2: for `current`, `git`, `artifact`, and `compiler-derived` evidence ranks first; for `intended` and `aspiration`, decisions and docs by owners rank first. Recency only breaks ties. The ranking is a hint to the reader, never a deletion.

## 6. The Jive Knowledge Graph interface

This interface is backend-agnostic. In Phase 0, Claude does these operations directly against the repo, following `BRAIN.md`. In Phase 1, a small HTTP service implements them, and the Jive Convex component calls that service.

```typescript
    text: string;
    types?: string[];
    predicates?: string[];

  }): Promise<SearchResult>;

  /** One entity with all its facts, plus incoming references from other entities. */
  get(id: EntityId): Promise<EntityView | null>;

  /** Walk typed edges. Depth capped at 3. */

    predicates?: string[];
    direction?: 'out' | 'in' | 'both';
    depth?: 1 | 2 | 3;

    writer: WriterId;
    message: string;           // becomes the commit message: why this was written
    entities?: EntityInput[];
    facts?: FactInput[];       // each names its subject entity
  }): Promise<{ commit: string; factIds: string[] }>;

  retract(q: { writer: WriterId; factId: string; reason: string }): Promise<{ commit: string }>;

  /** Facts whose evidence has changed since they were written. */

  fact: Fact;                                   // as in §4.2
  subject: EntityId;
  freshness: 'fresh' | 'stale' | 'unverifiable';
  contradictions: Fact[];                       // facts linked by `contradicts`, either direction

export interface EntityView {
  entity: { id: EntityId; type: string; name: string; aliases: string[]; summary?: string };
  facts: FactView[];
  incoming: Array<{ from: EntityId; factId: string; predicate: string }>;
}

  entities: EntityView[];
  facts: FactView[];
  code?: CodeHit[];          // from the Code Intelligence provider, if configured
```

- **`write.message` is required.** It records why a fact was written, in git history, at no extra cost.
- **There's no delete.** Retraction keeps history, and humans can still hard-edit the repo for genuine mistakes or sensitive data.
- **No business ID, permissions field, snapshots, or budgets.** Each one existed to serve a non-goal.

| Deliverable | Description |
|---|---|
| `brain` repo | Directory layout per §4.1, starter `schema/predicates.yaml`, and `BRAIN.md` conventions. |
| `brain validate` | CLI that checks frontmatter shape, required sources, known predicates, dangling references, and writer ownership against git authors. Runs as a pre-commit hook and in CI. |
| `brain stale` | CLI implementing the git and artifact checks in §5.1. Doc and message checks report `unverifiable` until connectors exist. |
| `brain index` | Builds a throwaway JSON index (entities, facts, backlinks) so `get` and `neighbors` are fast. Not committed. |

| Golden questions | 20 real DAT questions with expected entities and sources, used to judge whether the brain is actually useful. |

**Phase 1: interface service and Jive adapter.** A small HTTP service owns the repo and implements §6. Sourcegraph, if adopted, is wired in as the Code Intelligence provider.

- Write throughput from parallel workflows exceeds what one serialized writer handles.

| Item | Notes |
|---|---|

| **Sourcegraph availability and cost** | Not verified. Phase 0 doesn't depend on it, since Claude can grep local checkouts. |

2. **Staleness works:** after a commit changes a cited file, `brain stale` lists exactly the facts citing that file's old blob, and nothing else.

# Jive Knowledge Graph — Design

**Status:** Draft for review · **Date:** 2026-10-10 · **Author:** Alex Leung (with Claude)
**Supersedes:** `jive-memory-agent-handoff.md` (Codex, rev 0.2)

---

## 1. What we are building

Every Jive project gets one **brain**: a shared, durable body of knowledge that any agent working on that project can read and write. The ideal reader is a "super worker" who is simultaneously staff engineer, designer, TPM, and CEO, and therefore needs accurate knowledge of everything: how the code works, how the business works, who owns what, what was decided, what was promised, and what people intend to build.

Examples of projects and the knowledge their brains accumulate:

| Project | Knowledge comes from | Example facts |
|---|---|---|
| DAT (employer) | Code, Confluence, meetings, Slack, agent work | "Rate service X computes lane rates via Y", "Team Z owns X", "We committed to customer A by Oct 23" |
| Game decompilation (personal) | Binary, decompiled C, subagent results | "Function 0x4012F0 matches byte for byte", "Struct `Player` is 0x48 bytes" |

The Knowledge Graph is a **Jive interface**, in the same way that Message Board (Slack, Discord) and Task Board (Linear, Jira) are interfaces. Implementations are Convex components that act as thin adapters and call an external backend over HTTP. This document specifies the interface and recommends the backend.

**Immediate use:** before Jive launches, Alex uses the brain standalone. Claude reads DAT code and documents and writes into it, and agents get skills for querying it. Automated workflows (on commit, after meetings) come later and later move into Jive.

## 2. Requirements

What each requirement is, and why it exists:

| # | Requirement | Why |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | **One brain per project, domain-neutral.** Code and business knowledge live together and cross-link. | The super worker's questions span both ("which customer commitments depend on this service?"). |
| R2 | **Every fact records its evidence and how it was derived** (compiler, imported, human, model). | Accuracy. Many agents write over time and some will be wrong. A claim without a source can't be checked or challenged. |
| R3 | **Facts whose evidence has changed are detectable as possibly stale.** Agents and workflows do the fixing; the brain only points. | "Improve the graph on commit" requires knowing what the commit invalidated. |
| R4 | **Conflicting claims coexist with their evidence.** Nothing is overwritten by whoever wrote last. | A Slack message can't override what the code does. A reply of "you're wrong, here's the code reference" must win on evidence, not recency. |
| R5 | **Code structure is compiler-exact**, not LLM-guessed. | "A calls B" is either true or false, and a compiler knows which. |
| R6 | **Writers are attributed, and one writer can't silently destroy another's facts.** Bad writes can be rolled back by writer. | A misbehaving workflow should be containable. |
| R7 | **The interface is backend-agnostic**, so the Jive adapter stays thin. | Same pattern as other Jive interfaces. The backend can be swapped as needs grow. |
| R8 | **Usable this week.** | Alex needs to start building the DAT corpus now. |

### Claim kinds (nuance behind R4)

Claims about a system fall into three kinds, and which evidence is authoritative depends on the kind:

| Kind | Example | Authoritative evidence |
|---|---|---|
| `current` | "Retries use a fixed 5s delay" | Code and compiler output. Runtime data. |
| `intended` | "Retries should back off exponentially" | Design docs, ADRs, decisions by owners |
| `aspiration` | "We want a self-serve pricing API in 2027" | Roadmaps, strategy docs, leadership statements |

Code is authoritative on **what the system does**, not on **what it should do**. A Slack message saying "the retry logic is wrong" can't be rebutted by the code, because the code is the thing in dispute.

**Decision:** `kind` is an **optional** field. Writers set it when it's clear. Readers otherwise infer it from the source type: compiler output → `current`, design doc → `intended`, roadmap → `aspiration`. We'll formalize it further only if drift questions ("where does reality diverge from intent?") turn out to be common.

### Explicit non-goals

- **Read permissions.** Everything in a project's brain is visible to every agent and person using that project. In most companies, docs and code are broadly readable, so read restriction is the rare exception. The project boundary is the only wall.
- **Automatic truth adjudication.** The brain ranks claims by evidence but doesn't declare winners.
- **Automatic re-extraction.** The brain never calls an LLM, crawls a source, or fixes a fact by itself.
- **Copying code structure into the brain.** See §4.3.
- **The heavy machinery of the Codex design:** transitive atomic invalidation, snapshot publication, a three-clock temporal model, per-source ACLs, and one-container Postgres packaging. Each one solved a requirement we don't have.

## 3. Options considered

### 3.1 Candidates

**A. Graphiti** (open source, from Zep). A Python framework for temporal knowledge graphs. Per its README, it requires Neo4j, FalkorDB, or Neptune, plus an LLM and embedding API. It ingests text "episodes" and uses an LLM to extract entities and edges. It has an MCP server and a REST service, and it invalidates contradicted facts automatically while keeping their history.

**B. Zep.** The managed version of the Graphiti engine, with SLAs and a proprietary graph store.

**C. Brain-as-repo.** Knowledge is stored as structured text files in a git repository. Claude reads and writes it directly now, and a thin service exposes it through the interface later. Sourcegraph can optionally index it alongside the real code repos.

**D. Custom service.** A purpose-built database service, essentially a simplified Codex design.

### 3.2 Evaluation

| Requirement | A. Graphiti | B. Zep | C. Brain-as-repo | D. Custom |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1 domain-neutral, cross-linked | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| R2 evidence per fact | Partial: facts trace to episodes, not to exact quotes/versions you choose | Partial (same) | **Yes**: explicit source fields, plus git author, time, and message | Yes |
| R3 stale detection | Its own temporal invalidation, not source-version-based | Same | **Yes**: compare recorded source versions to current ones (§5) | Yes |
| R4 evidence-weighted conflicts | **Conflict:** it auto-invalidates contradicted facts. Whether that's recency- or LLM-driven needs verifying, but it isn't evidence-ranked. | Same | **Yes**: claims coexist, and rebuttals cite evidence | Yes |
| R5 compiler-exact code | No: LLM extraction | No | **Yes**, by linking to SCIP symbols (§4.3) | Yes |
| R6 writer attribution and rollback | Limited | Limited | **Yes**: one commit per write, and `git revert` by writer | Yes, but must be built |
| R7 behind a thin adapter | Yes (REST) | Yes (API) | Yes, once the service exists (Phase 1) | Yes |
| R8 usable this week | Yes, about an hour (estimate) | Yes, but it's a paid account | **Yes, today** | **No**: weeks |
| Write control | Low: an LLM decides what's stored | Low | **Full**: the writer writes exactly the fact | Full |
| Cost per write | One LLM call | Included in plan | Free | Free |
| Multi-hop graph queries | Strong | Strong | **Weak** until Phase 2's derived index | Strong |
| Many concurrent writers | Good | Good | **Merge friction** until Phase 1 serializes writes | Good |

The deciding factors:

1. **R4 rules out A and B as the system of record.** Their core feature, automatic contradiction invalidation, is the opposite of evidence-weighted coexistence. A Slack message could retire a code-backed fact.
2. **R2 and R5 favor exact writes over LLM extraction.** The brain's value is accuracy. Running every write through another model's interpretation adds an unaccountable error source.

4. **It's usable today, and it doesn't lock us in.** The interface (§6) hides the repo. If scale or graph-query needs outgrow it, Phase 2 adds a derived database index that is rebuilt from the repo, and the repo stays the source of truth.

Accepted weaknesses: multi-hop queries are slow or manual until Phase 2, and concurrent writers need a single writer service (Phase 1). Both are cheap to fix and neither blocks the DAT corpus.

### 4.1 Entities

An entity is anything worth knowing about: a person, team, organization, service, repository, decision, commitment, process, concept, function, or struct. Each entity is one file.

# Jive Knowledge Graph — Design

**Status:** Draft for review · **Date:** 2026-10-10 · **Author:** Alex Leung (with Claude)
**Supersedes:** `jive-memory-agent-handoff.md` (Codex, rev 0.2)

---

## 1. What we are building

Every Jive project gets one **brain**: a shared, durable body of knowledge that any agent working on that project can read and write. The ideal reader is a "super worker" who is simultaneously staff engineer, designer, TPM, and CEO, and therefore needs accurate knowledge of everything: how the code works, how the business works, who owns what, what was decided, what was promised, and what people intend to build.

Examples of projects and the knowledge their brains accumulate:

| Project | Knowledge comes from | Example facts |
|---|---|---|
| DAT (employer) | Code, Confluence, meetings, Slack, agent work | "Rate service X computes lane rates via Y", "Team Z owns X", "We committed to customer A by Oct 23" |
| Game decompilation (personal) | Binary, decompiled C, subagent results | "Function 0x4012F0 matches byte for byte", "Struct `Player` is 0x48 bytes" |

The Knowledge Graph is a **Jive interface**, in the same way that Message Board (Slack, Discord) and Task Board (Linear, Jira) are interfaces. Implementations are Convex components that act as thin adapters and call an external backend over HTTP. This document specifies the interface and recommends the backend.

**Immediate use:** before Jive launches, Alex uses the brain standalone. Claude reads DAT code and documents and writes into it, and agents get skills for querying it. Automated workflows (on commit, after meetings) come later and later move into Jive.

## 2. Requirements

What each requirement is, and why it exists:

| # | Requirement | Why |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | **One brain per project, domain-neutral.** Code and business knowledge live together and cross-link. | The super worker's questions span both ("which customer commitments depend on this service?"). |
| R2 | **Every fact records its evidence and how it was derived** (compiler, imported, human, model). | Accuracy. Many agents write over time and some will be wrong. A claim without a source can't be checked or challenged. |
| R3 | **Facts whose evidence has changed are detectable as possibly stale.** Agents and workflows do the fixing; the brain only points. | "Improve the graph on commit" requires knowing what the commit invalidated. |
| R4 | **Conflicting claims coexist with their evidence.** Nothing is overwritten by whoever wrote last. | A Slack message can't override what the code does. A reply of "you're wrong, here's the code reference" must win on evidence, not recency. |
| R5 | **Code structure is compiler-exact**, not LLM-guessed. | "A calls B" is either true or false, and a compiler knows which. |
| R6 | **Writers are attributed, and one writer can't silently destroy another's facts.** Bad writes can be rolled back by writer. | A misbehaving workflow should be containable. |
| R7 | **The interface is backend-agnostic**, so the Jive adapter stays thin. | Same pattern as other Jive interfaces. The backend can be swapped as needs grow. |
| R8 | **Usable this week.** | Alex needs to start building the DAT corpus now. |

### Claim kinds (nuance behind R4)

Claims about a system fall into three kinds, and which evidence is authoritative depends on the kind:

| Kind | Example | Authoritative evidence |
|---|---|---|
| `current` | "Retries use a fixed 5s delay" | Code and compiler output. Runtime data. |
| `intended` | "Retries should back off exponentially" | Design docs, ADRs, decisions by owners |
| `aspiration` | "We want a self-serve pricing API in 2027" | Roadmaps, strategy docs, leadership statements |

Code is authoritative on **what the system does**, not on **what it should do**. A Slack message saying "the retry logic is wrong" can't be rebutted by the code, because the code is the thing in dispute.

**Decision:** `kind` is an **optional** field. Writers set it when it's clear. Readers otherwise infer it from the source type: compiler output → `current`, design doc → `intended`, roadmap → `aspiration`. We'll formalize it further only if drift questions ("where does reality diverge from intent?") turn out to be common.

### Explicit non-goals

- **Read permissions.** Everything in a project's brain is visible to every agent and person using that project. In most companies, docs and code are broadly readable, so read restriction is the rare exception. The project boundary is the only wall.
- **Automatic truth adjudication.** The brain ranks claims by evidence but doesn't declare winners.
- **Automatic re-extraction.** The brain never calls an LLM, crawls a source, or fixes a fact by itself.
- **Copying code structure into the brain.** See §4.3.
- **The heavy machinery of the Codex design:** transitive atomic invalidation, snapshot publication, a three-clock temporal model, per-source ACLs, and one-container Postgres packaging. Each one solved a requirement we don't have.

## 3. Options considered

### 3.1 Candidates

**A. Graphiti** (open source, from Zep). A Python framework for temporal knowledge graphs. Per its README, it requires Neo4j, FalkorDB, or Neptune, plus an LLM and embedding API. It ingests text "episodes" and uses an LLM to extract entities and edges. It has an MCP server and a REST service, and it invalidates contradicted facts automatically while keeping their history.

**B. Zep.** The managed version of the Graphiti engine, with SLAs and a proprietary graph store.

**C. Brain-as-repo.** Knowledge is stored as structured text files in a git repository. Claude reads and writes it directly now, and a thin service exposes it through the interface later. Sourcegraph can optionally index it alongside the real code repos.

**D. Custom service.** A purpose-built database service, essentially a simplified Codex design.

### 3.2 Evaluation

| Requirement | A. Graphiti | B. Zep | C. Brain-as-repo | D. Custom |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1 domain-neutral, cross-linked | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| R2 evidence per fact | Partial: facts trace to episodes, not to exact quotes/versions you choose | Partial (same) | **Yes**: explicit source fields, plus git author, time, and message | Yes |
| R3 stale detection | Its own temporal invalidation, not source-version-based | Same | **Yes**: compare recorded source versions to current ones (§5) | Yes |
| R4 evidence-weighted conflicts | **Conflict:** it auto-invalidates contradicted facts. Whether that's recency- or LLM-driven needs verifying, but it isn't evidence-ranked. | Same | **Yes**: claims coexist, and rebuttals cite evidence | Yes |
| R5 compiler-exact code | No: LLM extraction | No | **Yes**, by linking to SCIP symbols (§4.3) | Yes |
| R6 writer attribution and rollback | Limited | Limited | **Yes**: one commit per write, and `git revert` by writer | Yes, but must be built |
| R7 behind a thin adapter | Yes (REST) | Yes (API) | Yes, once the service exists (Phase 1) | Yes |
| R8 usable this week | Yes, about an hour (estimate) | Yes, but it's a paid account | **Yes, today** | **No**: weeks |
| Write control | Low: an LLM decides what's stored | Low | **Full**: the writer writes exactly the fact | Full |
| Cost per write | One LLM call | Included in plan | Free | Free |
| Multi-hop graph queries | Strong | Strong | **Weak** until Phase 2's derived index | Strong |
| Many concurrent writers | Good | Good | **Merge friction** until Phase 1 serializes writes | Good |

### 3.3 Recommendation: C (brain-as-repo), behind the Jive interface from day one

The deciding factors:

1. **R4 rules out A and B as the system of record.** Their core feature, automatic contradiction invalidation, is the opposite of evidence-weighted coexistence. A Slack message could retire a code-backed fact.
2. **R2 and R5 favor exact writes over LLM extraction.** The brain's value is accuracy. Running every write through another model's interpretation adds an unaccountable error source.
3. **Git already provides most of what the Codex design built by hand:** an immutable history, attribution, diffs, review, time travel, and revert.
4. **It's usable today, and it doesn't lock us in.** The interface (§6) hides the repo. If scale or graph-query needs outgrow it, Phase 2 adds a derived database index that is rebuilt from the repo, and the repo stays the source of truth.

Accepted weaknesses: multi-hop queries are slow or manual until Phase 2, and concurrent writers need a single writer service (Phase 1). Both are cheap to fix and neither blocks the DAT corpus.

**When to revisit:** if Phase 2 triggers (§8) fire and a derived index isn't enough, re-evaluate D. Graphiti may still be useful as a **read-side helper** over the repo's content, but not as the system of record.

## 4. Data model

### 4.1 Entities

An entity is anything worth knowing about: a person, team, organization, service, repository, decision, commitment, process, concept, function, or struct. Each entity is one file.

```text
brain/
  entities/
    organization/acme.md
    person/alex-leung.md
    service/rate-engine.md
    decision/2026-09-rate-cache.md
  schema/            # predicate vocabulary + validator config
  BRAIN.md           # conventions for agents (the skill references this)
```

- **ID** is the file path without its extension, for example `service/rate-engine`. It's stable, readable, and greppable.
- **Types** are free strings with a recommended vocabulary in `schema/`. There's no hard-coded domain model.
- **Names aren't identities.** Two files that might be the same entity are linked with a `same-as` fact that carries evidence, never merged by name.

### 4.2 Facts

Facts live in the frontmatter of their **subject** entity's file. Prose below the frontmatter is a human- and LLM-readable summary, and it's also a fact (`predicate: summary`) with its own sources.

```markdown
---
id: service/rate-engine
type: service
name: Rate Engine
aliases: [rateengine, RE]
facts:
  - id: f-20261010-a1
    predicate: owned-by
    object: team/pricing-platform
    kind: current
    basis: imported
    writer: claude/dat-reader@1
    sources:
      - type: doc
        ref: confluence://PRICING/12345
        version: "v42"
        quote: "Pricing Platform team owns the Rate Engine."
  - id: f-20261010-a2
    predicate: retry-policy
    value: "fixed 5s delay, 3 attempts"
    kind: current
    basis: model-inferred
    writer: claude/dat-reader@1
    sources:
      - type: git
        repo: dat/rate-engine
        commit: 9f1c2ab
        path: src/client/retry.ts
        blob: 3b18e51
        lines: 12-30
  - id: f-20261010-a3
    predicate: retry-policy
    value: "exponential backoff"
    kind: intended
    basis: human-asserted
    writer: claude/dat-reader@1
    contradicts: [f-20261010-a2]
    sources:
      - type: message
        ref: slack://C0PRICING/1728400000.123
        version: original
        quote: "retry logic is wrong, it should back off exponentially"
---
The Rate Engine computes lane rates for ...
```

Field rules:

| Field | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | yes | Unique within the brain. Never reused. |
| `predicate` | yes | From the vocabulary in `schema/`. New predicates may be added, but the validator warns on unknown ones. |
| `object` / `value` | exactly one | `object` is an entity ID or code symbol (§4.3). `value` is a literal. |
| `kind` | no | `current`, `intended`, or `aspiration` (§2). |
| `basis` | yes | `compiler-derived`, `imported`, `human-asserted`, or `model-inferred`. This is a label, not proof. |
| `writer` | yes | Agent or workflow identity plus version. |
| `sources` | yes, ≥1 | Exact evidence (§5.1). A fact with no source is rejected. |
| `contradicts` | no | IDs of facts this one disputes. Both remain. |
| `status` | no | Absent means active. `retracted` (with `reason`) is set only by the fact's own writer or a human. |

**Ownership rule (R6):** a writer may edit or retract only facts it wrote. To dispute someone else's fact, it adds a new fact with `contradicts`. Humans may edit anything. The validator enforces this by comparing the `writer` field to the git author.

### 4.3 Code knowledge: link, don't copy

Compiler-exact structure (definitions, references, call sites, types) **stays in the code and its SCIP index**. It is not copied into the brain, which avoids a whole class of staleness: structural facts can't go stale if they're never duplicated.

The brain stores knowledge *about* code: architecture, intent, ownership, rationale, known bugs, and how a component relates to the business. It references code precisely:

- **File or region:** a `git` source with `repo`, `commit`, `path`, `blob`, and `lines`.
- **Symbol:** `object: "scip:<SCIP symbol string>"`, so a fact can point at an exact function or type in an exact package version.

Structural questions ("who calls `computeRate`?") go to code intelligence, either Sourcegraph or a local SCIP index. I recommend modeling that as its own Jive interface (Code Intelligence) rather than folding it into the Knowledge Graph. The Knowledge Graph's `search` can return code hits from that provider alongside brain facts.

## 5. Accuracy mechanics

### 5.1 Source types and how freshness is checked

| Source `type` | Identity fields | Version recorded | Freshness check |
|---|---|---|---|
| `git` | `repo`, `path`, optional `lines` | `commit` + `blob` (git blob SHA of the file) | Compare `blob` to the blob at the tracked branch's head. If it differs or the path is gone, the fact is stale. |
| `doc` | `ref` (Confluence, Google Doc, etc.) | the system's page version or last-modified | Compare against the current version through that system's API, when connected. Otherwise `unverifiable`. |
| `message` | `ref` (platform, channel, timestamp) | `original` or the edit timestamp | Usually immutable. Check edits where the platform exposes them. |
| `meeting` | `ref` (transcript ID), segment | transcript revision | Compare the revision. |
| `artifact` | `ref` (build output, binary hash, test report) | content hash | Compare the hash. |
| `fact` | another fact's `id` | that fact's last-changed commit | Stale if the cited fact changed or was retracted. This is one hop only, not a transitive closure. |

The **file-level blob check is deliberately conservative.** An unrelated edit elsewhere in the file also flags the fact. A false "maybe stale" costs an agent one re-check. A missed stale fact costs accuracy. Line-range-aware checking is a possible refinement, but not v1.

Every source also carries an optional `quote`: the exact text the claim rests on. It costs little and lets a reader verify the claim without fetching the source.

### 5.2 Staleness is computed, not stored

The brain doesn't keep a stale flag that has to stay in sync. `brain stale [--scope <path|repo|source>]` computes stale facts on demand by running the checks in §5.1. Reads attach `freshness: fresh | stale | unverifiable` to each returned fact. After a commit lands, a workflow runs `brain stale --scope repo:<name>` and re-derives what it finds. That's the "improve the graph on commit" loop.

### 5.3 Contradictions

When a read returns a fact that has `contradicts` links in either direction, it returns the whole cluster. Ranking within the cluster follows the authority table in §2: for `current`, `git`, `artifact`, and `compiler-derived` evidence ranks first; for `intended` and `aspiration`, decisions and docs by owners rank first. Recency only breaks ties. The ranking is a hint to the reader, never a deletion.

## 6. The Jive Knowledge Graph interface

```typescript
export interface KnowledgeGraph {
  /** Find entities and facts relevant to a question. Never calls an LLM. */
  search(q: {
    text: string;
    types?: string[];
    predicates?: string[];
    kinds?: Array<'current' | 'intended' | 'aspiration'>;
    limit?: number;            // default 20
  }): Promise<SearchResult>;

  /** One entity with all its facts, plus incoming references from other entities. */
  get(id: EntityId): Promise<EntityView | null>;

  /** Walk typed edges. Depth capped at 3. */
  neighbors(q: {
    from: EntityId;
    predicates?: string[];
    direction?: 'out' | 'in' | 'both';
    depth?: 1 | 2 | 3;
  }): Promise<EntityView[]>;

  /** Add or update entities and facts. Rejects unsourced facts and edits to other writers' facts. */
  write(batch: {
    writer: WriterId;
    message: string;           // becomes the commit message: why this was written
    entities?: EntityInput[];
    facts?: FactInput[];       // each names its subject entity
  }): Promise<{ commit: string; factIds: string[] }>;

  /** Retract one of the caller's own facts. History is preserved. */
  retract(q: { writer: WriterId; factId: string; reason: string }): Promise<{ commit: string }>;

  /** Facts whose evidence has changed since they were written. */
  stale(q?: { scope?: string; cursor?: string; limit?: number }): Promise<StaleReport>;
}

export interface FactView {
  fact: Fact;                                   // as in §4.2
  subject: EntityId;
  freshness: 'fresh' | 'stale' | 'unverifiable';
  contradictions: Fact[];                       // facts linked by `contradicts`, either direction
}

export interface EntityView {
  entity: { id: EntityId; type: string; name: string; aliases: string[]; summary?: string };
  facts: FactView[];
  incoming: Array<{ from: EntityId; factId: string; predicate: string }>;
}

export interface SearchResult {
  entities: EntityView[];
  facts: FactView[];
  code?: CodeHit[];          // from the Code Intelligence provider, if configured
}
```

content.text:
The design doc is ready. It's about a third the length of Codex's, and every requirement and decision in it traces back to something you said.

**Recommendation:** make the brain a git repo of structured text files, sitting behind a six-method Jive interface from day one. Git gives you provenance, history, and rollback by writer without building them. You can start this week with Claude reading and writing the files directly. A small HTTP service and the Convex adapter come next, and a database index only once real usage shows it's needed. The repo stays the source of truth throughout.

**Calls most worth pushing back on:**

1. **I ruled Graphiti and Zep out as the main store.** Their core feature automatically retires facts that get contradicted, which is the opposite of your "a Slack message can't override the code". I only know that mechanism from Graphiti's README, so it should be checked.
2. **Code structure stays in the code and its SCIP index.** The brain links to exact files and symbols rather than copying them. Copied structure is exactly what goes stale.
3. **Staleness is checked per file.** If a cited file changes at all, the fact is flagged. That over-flags on unrelated edits, which I think is the right trade for accuracy.
4. **The DAT brain needs a DAT-approved home,** such as DAT's GitHub organization, not a personal account. That's your call to confirm.

I couldn't commit the doc to git because there's no repo in this session. Read it through and tell me what to change before we plan the build.

message.content: I think you might have indexed too hard on "current", "intended" and "aspiration". Couldn't there be all sorts of other categoriztions? Or do you think that's actually the right way to think about facts in a business?

content.text:
I think you're right that I over-indexed on it.

There are many other ways to slice business facts. You could sort by certainty (confirmed, rumored, disputed), by time (what was true, what is, what will be), or by speech act (a decision, a commitment, an opinion, an open question). You could also sort by scope (one team's view versus company policy). Each is real, and none is obviously the master axis.

The underlying distinction I was grabbing at is real: describing how things *are* versus saying how they *should be*. It matters because it changes which evidence settles a dispute. The code settles "what does retry do". It doesn't settle "what should retry do". So the insight was worth having in the conversation.

Where I went wrong was turning one exchange into schema. I added a `kind` field and a hard-coded table saying which evidence wins for each kind. That freezes one taxonomy into the brain when nobody has used it yet.

I think the better design is simpler. Facts keep their sources and basis, contradictions stay linked, and the brain returns the whole disagreement with evidence attached. The reading agent weighs it. An LLM that can see "this claim cites the code at line 30, that one cites a Slack message saying it *should* behave differently" can tell those apart without a field telling it to. Most of the distinction also already lives in the predicate and the wording of the fact itself.

So I'd remove `kind`, remove the ranking rules, and keep a short note in the conventions doc reminding writers to phrase normative claims as normative ("should", "decided", "plan to"). If drift questions later prove common, a field can come back based on real usage.

Want me to make that edit to the doc?

message.content: Facts should probably also come with a timestamp

content.text:
Agreed. Right now a write time is only recoverable from git history, and agents reading facts won't see it. It should be on the fact itself.

There are two different times, and I'd keep both but nothing more:

- **When the brain learned it** (`recorded_at`). Set automatically on write.
- **When the evidence is from** (`at` on each source): the Slack message's timestamp, the commit date, the meeting date. This one usually matters more. "Alex owns Acme" from a message two years ago is weaker than the same claim from last week, even if both were written into the brain today. It's mostly filled in automatically, because the source already carries it.

I'd skip a "valid from / valid until" range for now. That's the part of Codex's three-clock model that made writers do extra work and was rarely knowable. When a claim really has a time bound, like a deadline or "until Q3", the fact can just say so.

Want me to make both edits to the doc now: add the timestamps, and drop the `kind` field and ranking rules?

message.content: Did you not want source graph as an option?

content.text:
It's in the doc, but I folded it in rather than listing it as its own option, and I should have been clearer about why.

Sourcegraph appears in two places. It can index the brain repo alongside DAT's code repos (option C), and it's the recommended Code Intelligence provider for structural questions like "who calls `computeRate`" (§4.3). I didn't put it in the comparison table on its own because it isn't a store agents write knowledge into. It reads and searches repos. On its own it covers the code half of the brain but not the business half. Paired with a brain repo it covers both, which is what option C describes.

I did underweight it, though, by making it an optional later addition. At DAT, with many repos, cross-repo search, SCIP navigation, and its MCP server would make reads much better from day one. Grepping local checkouts doesn't scale to that. I deferred it only because I don't know its cost or whether you have access.

So the deciding fact is whether DAT already runs Sourcegraph. If it does, I'd make it part of Phase 0 and say so explicitly in the doc. Do you know if it does?

# SCIP Code Intelligence Protocol

SCIP (pronunciation: "skip") is a language-agnostic protocol
for indexing source code,
which can be used to power code navigation functionality
such as Go to definition, Find references, and Find implementations.

This repository includes:

- A [Protobuf schema for SCIP](./scip.proto).
- Rich Go and Rust bindings for SCIP: These include many utility functions
  to help build tooling on top of SCIP.
- Auto-generated bindings for TypeScript and Haskell.
- The [`scip` CLI](./docs/CLI.md), which makes SCIP indexes
  a breeze to work with.

If you're interested in better understanding the motivation behind SCIP,
check out the [announcement blog post](https://about.sourcegraph.com/blog/announcing-scip) and the [design doc](./docs/DESIGN.md).

If you're interested in writing a new indexer that emits SCIP,
check out our documentation on
[how to write an indexer](https://docs.sourcegraph.com/code_intelligence/explanations/writing_an_indexer).
Also, check out the [Debugging section][] in the Development docs.

If you're interested in consuming SCIP data,
you can either use one of the [provided language bindings](https://github.com/scip-code/scip/tree/main/bindings),
or generate code for the [SCIP Protobuf schema](./scip.proto)
using the Protobuf toolchain for your language ecosystem.
Also, check out the [Debugging section][] in the Development docs.

[debugging section]: ./docs/Development.md#debugging

## Tools using SCIP

Several indexers currently emit SCIP data:

- [scip-java](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-java): Java, Scala, Kotlin
- [scip-typescript](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-typescript): TypeScript, JavaScript
- [rust-analyzer](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer): Rust
- [scip-clang](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-clang): C++, C
- [scip-ruby](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-ruby): Ruby
- [scip-python](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-python): Python
- [scip-dotnet](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-dotnet): C#, Visual Basic
- [scip-dart](https://github.com/Workiva/scip-dart): Dart
- [scip-php](https://github.com/davidrjenni/scip-php): PHP
- [debian-lsp](https://github.com/jelmer/debian-lsp): Debian packaging files

For more details about indexers,
see the [Sourcegraph documentation](https://docs.sourcegraph.com/code_navigation/references/indexers).

Other tools which use SCIP include the [Sourcegraph CLI](https://github.com/sourcegraph/src-cli),
and the SCIP CLI in this repo.

## Installing the `scip` CLI

You can find binaries for the `scip` CLI tool [here](https://github.com/scip-code/scip/releases).
You can also compile a binary locally using:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/scip-code/scip.git --depth=1
cd scip
go build ./cmd/scip
```

You can consult the [CLI reference](docs/CLI.md) or `--help` for usage information.

## Contributing

We welcome questions, suggestions as well as code and docs contributions.

For submitting contributions, check out [Development.md](./docs/Development.md)
to better understand project structure and common workflows.

Contributors should abide by the [Code of Conduct](https://scip-code.org/code-of-conduct.html).

```
USAGE:
```
```
   scip snapshot [options]

DESCRIPTION:
   The snapshot subcommand generates snapshot files which
   can be use for inspecting the output of an index in a
   visual way. Occurrences are marked with caret signs (^)
   and symbol information.

   For testing a SCIP indexer, you can either use this subcommand
   along with 'git diff' or equivalent, or you can use the dedicated
   'test' subcommand for more targeted checks.


OPTIONS:
```

```
NAME:

USAGE:
   scip test [options]

DESCRIPTION:
   Validates whether the SCIP data present in an index
   matches that specified in human-readable test files, using syntax
   similar to the 'snapshot' subcommand. Test file syntax reference:

       https://github.com/scip-code/scip/blob/v0.10.0
   /docs/test_file_format.md

   The test files are located based on the relative_path field
   in the SCIP document, interpreted relative to the the directory
   the CLI is invoked in.

   If you want to instead check all the data in a SCIP index,
   use the 'snapshot' subcommand.

OPTIONS:
   --from string                                              Path to SCIP index file (default: "index.scip")
   --comment-syntax string                                    Comment syntax to use for snapshot files (default: "//")
   --filter string, -f string [ --filter string, -f string ]  Explicit list of test files to check. Can be specified multiple times. If not specified, all files are tested.
   --check-documents                                          Whether or not to validate whether every file in the test directory has a correlating document in the SCIP index.
   --help, -h                                                 show help
```

```

DESCRIPTION:

OPTIONS:
```

```
   --cpu-profile string  Path to output prof file
   --help, -h            show help
```

content.text:
Yes. SCIP itself is free and separate from Sourcegraph. I checked the SCIP repo:

- **SCIP is an open protocol.** The repo ships a protobuf schema, bindings for Go, Rust, TypeScript, and Haskell, and a `scip` CLI.
- **Open-source indexers exist** for Java/Scala/Kotlin, TypeScript/JavaScript, Rust (via rust-analyzer), C/C++, Ruby, Python, C#/VB, Dart, and PHP. Go isn't listed in the README, so I wouldn't assume coverage there without checking.
- **The CLI has an experimental command that converts an index to SQLite** (`scip expt-convert`). One catch: occurrences are stored as opaque blobs, so answering "find references" from that database means decoding them. It's a starting point, not a finished query layer.

So the cheap version of what Sourcegraph gives you:

1. Run the matching indexer over each DAT repo on commit, producing one `index.scip` per repo.
2. Load those indexes into a small code-intelligence tool, either built on the TypeScript bindings or on the SQLite conversion. That tool answers definition, references, and implementations, including across repos.
3. Use ripgrep over local checkouts for plain text search. From memory, there's also an open-source code search engine called Zoekt, which Sourcegraph uses internally, if you outgrow ripgrep. I haven't checked its current state.

That's a modest build, and it fits the doc's existing plan: Code Intelligence as its own Jive interface, with the brain linking to SCIP symbols. The difference is the provider becomes a self-hosted tool instead of Sourcegraph.

The thing that decides how well this works is which languages DAT's code is in, because coverage varies by indexer. What are the main ones?

content.text:
Yes, I think you're right, and it's more consistent with your own framing.

The interface should describe what an agent can ask. How it gets answered is the implementation's business. An agent asking "what depends on the Acme commitment?" shouldn't have to know that part of the answer comes from stored facts and part from a compiler index. If I split them, every agent has to know about two systems and stitch the answers together. The cross-cutting questions are the whole point of a super-worker's brain, and they would be the hardest to answer.

Folded in, it looks like this:

- **Code symbols are entities** like any other, with IDs like `scip:<symbol>`. `get` on a function returns its definition location plus whatever the brain knows about it: owner, intent, known bugs.
- **Code relationships are edges**: `code:calls`, `code:references`, `code:implements`. The implementation computes them from SCIP indexes instead of storing them. To the agent, `neighbors` works the same whether an edge was written by Claude or derived by a compiler.
- **Code's freshness comes for free.** Derived edges always reflect the indexed commit, so they can't go stale the way written facts can.
- **Projects without code**, like a purely business project, just have no code sources. Nothing in the interface changes.

The one cost is fanout. A common utility function might have thousands of references, so `neighbors` needs firm result limits and paging. The interface should have that anyway.

That's three changes to the doc now:

1. Drop `kind` and the ranking rules.
2. Add both timestamps.
3. Fold code intelligence into the implementation.

Want me to make them?

content.text:
You're right to call it out. "One omniscient brain" points straight at one interface, and I split it anyway.

My best account of what happened: I divided things by what answers the question (Sourcegraph and SCIP on one side, stored facts on the other) rather than by what the agent needs. It's the same mistake I made earlier when I tied the design to Convex's search features. I let the shape of the implementation leak into the interface. Both times I was reasoning from the tools I had just looked at rather than from what you said you wanted, and the result fell short of your intent.

The fix isn't just this one edit. I'd go back through the whole doc and test each decision against "one brain that knows everything accurately, for any project." I'd cut or change anything that splits the brain or exposes how it works inside. I suspect there's at least one more instance. The interface still has `code?: CodeHit[]` as a separate result type, which is the same split in miniature.

If that works for you, I'll make the three changes plus that review pass, and tell you what else I find.
