# [Simon Willison’s Weblog](https://simonwillison.net/)

[Newsletter](https://simonwillison.net/newsletters/)

**Sponsored by:** Pomerium — Static OAuth scopes won't stop AI agent breakouts. [Upgrade to Pomerium's agentic access management trusted by NVIDIA and OpenAI](https://fandf.co/4hJeKAm)

## Embeddings: What they are and why they matter

23rd October 2023

Embeddings are a really neat trick that often come wrapped in a pile of intimidating jargon.

If you can make it through that jargon, they unlock powerful and exciting techniques that can be applied to all sorts of interesting problems.

I gave a talk about embeddings at [PyBay 2023](https://pybay.com/). This article represents an improved version of that talk, which should stand alone even without watching the video.

If you’re not yet familiar with embeddings I hope to give you everything you need to get started applying them to real-world problems.

In this article:

- [The 38 minute video version](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Oct/23/embeddings/#the-38-minute-video-version)
- [What are embeddings?](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Oct/23/embeddings/#what-are-embeddings)
- [Related content using embeddings](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Oct/23/embeddings/#related-content-using-embeddings)
- [Exploring how these things work with Word2Vec](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Oct/23/embeddings/#exploring-how-these-things-work-with-word2vec)
- [Calculating embeddings using my LLM tool](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Oct/23/embeddings/#calculating-embeddings-using-my-llm-tool)
- [Vibes-based search](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Oct/23/embeddings/#vibes-based-search)
- [Embeddings for code using Symbex](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Oct/23/embeddings/#embeddings-for-code-using-symbex)
- [Embedding text and images together using CLIP](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Oct/23/embeddings/#embedding-text-and-images-together-using-clip)
- [Faucet Finder: finding faucets with CLIP](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Oct/23/embeddings/#faucet-finder-finding-faucets-with-clip)
- [Clustering embeddings](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Oct/23/embeddings/#clustering-embeddings)
- [Visualize in 2D with Principal Component Analysis](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Oct/23/embeddings/#visualize-in-2d-with-principal-component-analysis)
- [Scoring sentences using average locations](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Oct/23/embeddings/#scoring-sentences-using-average-locations)
- [Answering questions with Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Oct/23/embeddings/#answering-questions-with-retrieval-augmented-generation)
- [Q&A](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Oct/23/embeddings/#qa)
- [Further reading](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Oct/23/embeddings/#embeddings-further-reading)

#### The 38 minute video version

Here’s [a video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ArnMdc-ICCM&t=50s) of the talk that I gave at PyBay:

[https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/ArnMdc-ICCM?start=50](https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/ArnMdc-ICCM?start=50)

The audio quality of the official video wasn’t great due to an issue with the microphone, but I ran that audio through Adobe’s [Enhance Speech tool](https://podcast.adobe.com/enhance) and uploaded my own video with the enhanced audio to YouTube.

#### What are embeddings?

Embeddings are a technology that’s adjacent to the wider field of Large Language Models—the technology behind ChatGPT and Gemini and Claude.

![On the left, a blog entry titled Storing and serving related documents with oepnai-to-sqlite and embeddings. On the right, a JSON array of floating point numbers, with the caption Fixed zise: 300, 1000, 1536...](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/embeddings.002.jpeg)

Embeddings are based around one trick: take a piece of content—in this case [a blog entry](https://til.simonwillison.net/llms/openai-embeddings-related-content)—and turn that piece of content into an array of floating point numbers.

The key thing about that array is that it will always be the same length, no matter how long the content is. The length is defined by the embedding model you are using—an array might be 300, or 1,000, or 1,536 numbers long.

The best way to think about this array of numbers is to imagine it as co-ordinates in a very weird multi-dimensional space.

It’s hard to visualize 1,536 dimensional space, so here’s a 3D visualization of the same idea:

![a 3D chart showing a location in many-multi-dimensional space. 400 randomly placed red dots are scattered around the chart.](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/embeddings.003.jpeg)

Why place content in this space? Because we can learn interesting things about that content based on its location—in particular, based on what else is nearby.

The location within the space represents the semantic meaning of the content, according to the embedding model’s weird, mostly incomprehensible understanding of the world. It might capture colors, shapes, concepts or all sorts of other characteristics of the content that has been embedded.

Nobody fully understands what those individual numbers mean, but we know that their locations can be used to find out useful things about the content.

#### Related content using embeddings

One of the first problems I solved with embeddings was to build a “related content” feature for [my TIL blog](https://til.simonwillison.net/). I wanted to be able to show a list of related articles at the bottom of each page.

I did this using embeddings—in this case, I used the OpenAI `text-embedding-ada-002` model, which is available [via their API](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/embeddings).

I currently have 472 articles on my site. I calculated the 1,536 dimensional embedding vector (array of floating point numbers) for each of those articles, and stored those vectors in my site’s SQLite database.

Now, if I want to find related articles for a given article, I can calculate the *cosine similarity* between the embedding vector for that article and every other article in the database, then return the 10 closest matches by distance.

There’s an example at [the bottom of this page](https://til.simonwillison.net/sqlite/sqlite-tg#related). The top five related articles for [Geospatial SQL queries in SQLite using TG, sqlite-tg and datasette-sqlite-tg](https://til.simonwillison.net/sqlite/sqlite-tg) are:

- [Geopoly in SQLite](https://til.simonwillison.net/sqlite/geopoly)—2023-01-04
- [Viewing GeoPackage data with SpatiaLite and Datasette](https://til.simonwillison.net/spatialite/viewing-geopackage-data-with-spatialite-and-datasette)—2022-12-11
- [Using SQL with GDAL](https://til.simonwillison.net/gis/gdal-sql)—2023-03-09
- [KNN queries with SpatiaLite](https://til.simonwillison.net/spatialite/knn)—2021-05-16
- [GUnion to combine geometries in SpatiaLite](https://til.simonwillison.net/spatialite/gunion-to-combine-geometries)—2022-04-12

That’s a pretty good list!

Here’s [the Python function](https://github.com/simonw/llm/blob/bf229945fe57036fa75e8105e59d9e506a720156/llm/__init__.py#L252C1-L256C53) I’m using to calculate those cosine similarity distances:

```
def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    dot_product = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    magnitude_a = sum(x * x for x in a) ** 0.5
    magnitude_b = sum(x * x for x in b) ** 0.5
    return dot_product / (magnitude_a * magnitude_b)
```

My TIL site runs on my [Datasette](https://datasette.io/) Python framework, which supports building sites on top of a SQLite database. I wrote more about how that works in [the Baked Data architectural pattern](https://simonwillison.net/2021/Jul/28/baked-data/).

You can browse the SQLite table that stores the calculated embeddings at [tils/embeddings](https://til.simonwillison.net/tils/embeddings).

![Screenshot of the embeddings table in Datasette, it has 472, rows each of which consists of a text ID and a binary 6.144 bytes embedding](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/til-simonwillison-net-tils-embeddings.png)

Those are binary values. We can [run this SQL query](https://til.simonwillison.net/tils?sql=select+id%2C+hex%28embedding%29+from+embeddings) to view them as hexadecimal:

```
select id, hex(embedding) from embeddings
```

![Running that SQL query in Datasette returns text IDs and long hexadecimal strings for each embedding](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/til-simonwillison-net-tils.png)

That’s still not very readable though. We can use the `llm_embed_decode()` custom SQL function to turn them into a JSON array:

```
select id, llm_embed_decode(embedding) from embeddings limit 10
```

[Try that here](https://til.simonwillison.net/tils?sql=select+id%2C+llm_embed_decode%28embedding%29+from+embeddings+limit+10). It shows that each article is accompanied by that array of 1,536 floating point numbers.

![Now the SQL query returns a JSON array of floating point numbers for each ID](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/til-simonwillison-net-tils.1.png)

We can use another custom SQL function, `llm_embed_cosine(vector1, vector2)`, to calculate those cosine distances and find the most similar content.

That SQL function [is defined here](https://github.com/simonw/datasette-llm-embed/blob/ebded67fa9ee19db2c4b1badb1895cef0d58ac4a/datasette_llm_embed.py#L22-L26) in my [datasette-llm-embed](https://datasette.io/plugins/datasette-llm-embed) plugin.

Here’s a query returning the five most similar articles to my SQLite TG article:

```
select
  id,
  llm_embed_cosine(
    embedding,
    (
      select
        embedding
      from
        embeddings
      where
        id = 'sqlite_sqlite-tg.md'
    )
  ) as score
from
  embeddings
order by
  score desc
limit 5
```

[Executing that query](https://til.simonwillison.net/tils?sql=select%0D%0A++id%2C%0D%0A++llm_embed_cosine%28%0D%0A++++embedding%2C%0D%0A++++%28%0D%0A++++++select%0D%0A++++++++embedding%0D%0A++++++from%0D%0A++++++++embeddings%0D%0A++++++where%0D%0A++++++++id+%3D+%27sqlite_sqlite-tg.md%27%0D%0A++++%29%0D%0A++%29+as+score%0D%0Afrom%0D%0A++embeddings%0D%0Aorder+by%0D%0A++score+desc%0D%0Alimit+5) returns the following results:

| id                                                                   | score              |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ |
| sqlite\_sqlite-tg.md                                                 | 1.0                |
| sqlite\_geopoly.md                                                   | 0.8817322855676049 |
| spatialite\_viewing-geopackage-data-with-spatialite-and-datasette.md | 0.8813094978399854 |
| gis\_gdal-sql.md                                                     | 0.8799581261326747 |
| spatialite\_knn.md                                                   | 0.8692992294266506 |

As expected, the similarity between the article and itself is 1.0. The other articles are all related to geospatial SQL queries in SQLite.

This query takes around 400ms to execute. To speed things up, I pre-calculate the top 10 similarities for every article and store them in a separate table called [tils/similarities](https://til.simonwillison.net/tils/similarities).

![The similarities table has 4,922 rows each with an id, other_id and score column.](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/til-simonwillison-net-tils-similarities.png)

I wrote a Python function to [look up related documents from that table](https://github.com/simonw/til/blob/a244856c72000760c2939550ae2a78266dee4f07/plugins/template_vars.py#L21-L37) and [called it from the template](https://github.com/simonw/til/blob/a244856c72000760c2939550ae2a78266dee4f07/templates/pages/%7Btopic%7D/%7Bslug%7D.html#L37-L45) that’s used to render the article page.

My [Storing and serving related documents with openai-to-sqlite and embeddings](https://til.simonwillison.net/llms/openai-embeddings-related-content) TIL explains how this all works in detail, including how GitHub Actions are used to fetch new embeddings [as part of the build script](https://github.com/simonw/til/blob/a244856c72000760c2939550ae2a78266dee4f07/.github/workflows/build.yml#L67-L75) that deploys the site.

I used the OpenAI embeddings API for this project. It’s extremely inexpensive—for my TIL website I embedded around 402,500 tokens, which at $0.0001 / 1,000 tokens comes to $0.04—just 4 cents!

It’s really easy to use: you POST it some text along with your API key, it gives you back that JSON array of floating point numbers.

![Screenshot of curl against api.openai.com/v1/embeddings sending a Bearer token header and a JSON body specifying input text and the text-embedding-ada-002 model. The API responds with a JSON list of numbers.](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/embeddings.006.jpeg)

But... it’s a proprietary model. A few months ago OpenAI [shut down some of their older embeddings models](https://openai.com/blog/gpt-4-api-general-availability#deprecation-of-older-embeddings-models), which is a problem if you’ve stored large numbers of embeddings from those models since you’ll need to recalculate them against a supported model if you want to be able to embed anything else new.

![Screenshot of the OpenAI First-generation text embedding models list, showing the shutdown date of 4th April 2024 for 7 legacy models.](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/embeddings.007.jpeg)

To OpenAI’s credit, they did promise to “cover the financial cost of users re-embedding content with these new models.”—but it’s still a reason to be cautious about relying on proprietary models.

The good news is that there are extremely powerful openly licensed models which you can run on your own hardware, avoiding any risk of them being shut down. We’ll talk about that more in a moment.

#### Exploring how these things work with Word2Vec

Google Research put out an influential paper 10 years ago describing an early embedding model they created called Word2Vec.

That paper is [Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781), dated 16th January 2013. It’s a paper that helped kick off widespread interest in embeddings.

Word2Vec is a model that takes single words and turns them into a list of 300 numbers. That list of numbers captures something about the meaning of the associated word.

This is best illustrated by a demo.

[turbomaze.github.io/word2vecjson](https://turbomaze.github.io/word2vecjson/) is an interactive tool put together by [Anthony Liu](https://anthony.ai/) with a 10,000 word subset of the Word2Vec corpus. You can view [this JavaScript file](https://turbomaze.github.io/word2vecjson/data/wordvecs10000.js) to see the JSON for those 10,000 words and their associated 300-long arrays of numbers.

![Screenshot of the Word to Vec JS Demo showing the results for france and the algebra results for germany + paris - france](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/word2vec.jpg)

Search for a word to find similar words based on cosine distance to their Word2Vec representation. For example, the word “france” returns the following related results:

| word    | similarity         |
| ------- | ------------------ |
| france  | 1                  |
| french  | 0.7000748343471224 |
| belgium | 0.6933180492111168 |
| paris   | 0.6334910653433325 |
| germany | 0.627075617939471  |
| italy   | 0.6135215284228007 |
| spain   | 0.6064218103692152 |

That’s a mixture of french things and European geography.

A really interesting thing you can do here is perform arithmetic on these vectors.

Take the vector for “germany”, add “paris” and subtract “france”. The resulting vector is closest to “berlin”!

Something about this model has captured the idea of nationalities and geography to the point that you can use arithmetic to explore additional facts about the world.

Word2Vec was trained on 1.6 billion words of content. The embedding models we use today are trained on much larger datasets and capture a much richer understanding of the underlying relationships.

#### Calculating embeddings using my LLM tool

I’ve been building a command-line utility and Python library called [LLM](https://llm.datasette.io/).

You can read more about LLM here:

- [llm, ttok and strip-tags—CLI tools for working with ChatGPT and other LLMs](https://simonwillison.net/2023/May/18/cli-tools-for-llms/)
- [The LLM CLI tool now supports self-hosted language models via plugins](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Jul/12/llm/)
- [LLM now provides tools for working with embeddings](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Sep/4/llm-embeddings/)
- [Build an image search engine with llm-clip, chat with models with llm chat](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Sep/12/llm-clip-and-chat/)

LLM is a tool for working with Large Language Models. You can install it like this:

```
pip install llm
```

Or via Homebrew:

```
brew install llm
```

You can use it as a command-line tool for interacting with LLMs, or as [a Python library](https://llm.datasette.io/en/stable/python-api.html).

Out of the box it can work with the OpenAI API. Set [an API key](https://llm.datasette.io/en/stable/setup.html#saving-and-using-stored-keys) and you can run commands like this:

```
llm 'ten fun names for a pet pelican'
```

Where it gets really fun is when you start [installing plugins](https://llm.datasette.io/en/stable/plugins/index.html). There are plugins that add entirely new language models to it, including models that run directly on your own machine.

A few months ago [I extended LLM](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Sep/4/llm-embeddings/) to support plugins that can run embedding models as well.

Here’s how to run the catchily titled [all-MiniLM-L6-v2](https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2) model using LLM:

![Slide showing the commands listed below](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/embeddings.014.jpeg)

First, we install `llm` and then use that to install the [llm-sentence-transformers](https://github.com/simonw/llm-sentence-transformers) plugin—a wrapper around the [SentenceTransformers](https://www.sbert.net/) library.

```
pip install llm
llm install llm-sentence-transformers
```

Next we need to register the `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` model. This will download the model from Hugging Face to your computer:

```
llm sentence-transformers register all-MiniLM-L6-v2
```

We can test that out by embedding a single sentence like this:

```
llm embed -m sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 \
  -c 'Hello world'
```

This outputs a JSON array that starts like this:

`[-0.03447725251317024, 0.031023245304822922, 0.006734962109476328, 0.026108916848897934, -0.03936201333999634, ...`

Embeddings like this on their own aren’t very interesting—we need to store and compare them to start getting useful results.

LLM can store embeddings in a “collection”—a SQLite table. The [embed-multi command](https://llm.datasette.io/en/stable/embeddings/cli.html#llm-embed-multi) can be used to embed multiple pieces of content at once and store them in a collection.

That’s what this next command does:

```
llm embed-multi readmes \
  --model sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 \
  --files ~/ '**/README.md' --store
```

Here we are populating a collection called “readmes”.

The `--files` option takes two arguments: a directory to search and a glob pattern to match against filenames. In this case I’m searching my home directory recursively for any file named `README.md`.

The `--store` option causes LLM to store the raw text in the SQLite table in addition to the embedding vector.

This command took around 30 minutes to run on my computer, but it worked! I now have a collection called `readmes` with 16,796 rows—one for each `README.md` file it found in my home directory.

#### Vibes-based search

Now that we have a collection of embeddings, we can run searches against it using the [llm similar command](https://llm.datasette.io/en/stable/embeddings/cli.html#llm-similar):

![A terminal running llm similar and piping the results through jq](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/embeddings.015.jpeg)

```
llm similar readmes -c 'sqlite backup tools' | jq .id
```

We are asking for items in the `readmes` collection that are similar to the embedding vector for the phrase “sqlite backup tools”.

This command outputs JSON by default, which includes the full text of the README files since we stored them using `--store` earlier.

Piping the results through `jq .id` causes the command to output just the IDs of the matching rows.

The top matching results are:

```
"sqlite-diffable/README.md"
"sqlite-dump/README.md"
"ftstri/salite/ext/repair/README.md"
"simonw/README.md"
"sqlite-generate/README.md"
"sqlite-history/README.md"
"dbf-to-sqlite/README.md"
"ftstri/sqlite/ext/README.md"
"sqlite-utils/README.md"
"ftstri/sqlite/README.md'
```

These are good results! Each of these READMEs either describes a tool for working with SQLite backups or a project that relates to backups ins ome way.

What’s interesting about this is that it’s not guaranteed that the term “backups” appeared directly in the text of those READMEs. The content is semantically similar to that phrase, but might not be an exact textual match.

We can call this semantic search. I like to think of it as **vibes-based search**.

The vibes of those READMEs relate to our search term, according to this weird multi-dimensional space representation of the meaning of words.

This is absurdly useful. If you’ve ever built a search engine for a website, you know that exact matches don’t always help people find what they are looking for.

We can use this kind of semantic search to build better search engines for a whole bunch of different kinds of content.

#### Embeddings for code using Symbex

Another tool I’ve been building is called [Symbex](https://github.com/simonw/symbex). It’s a tool for exploring the symbols in a Python codebase.

I [originally built it](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Jun/18/symbex/) to help quickly find Python functions and classes and pipe them into LLMs to help explain and rewrite them.

Then I realized that I could use it to calculate embeddings for all of the functions in a codebase, and use those embeddings to build a code search engine.

I added a feature that could output JSON or CSV representing the symbols it found, using the same output format that `llm embed-multi` can use as an input.

Here’s how I built a collection of all of the functions in my [Datasette](https://github.com/simonw/datasette) project, using a newly released model called [gte-tiny](https://huggingface.co/TaylorAI/gte-tiny)—just a 60MB file!

```
llm sentence-transformers register TaylorAI/gte-tiny

cd datasette/datasette

symbex '*' '*:*' --nl | \
  llm embed-multi functions - \
  --model sentence-transformers/TaylorAI/gte-tiny \
  --format nl \
  --store
```

`symbex '*' '*:*' --nl` finds all functions (`*`) and class methods (the `*:*` pattern) in the current directory and outputs them as newline-delimited JSON.

The `llm embed-multi ... --format nl` command expects newline-delimited JSON as input, so we can pipe the output of `symbex` directly into it.

This defaults to storing the embeddings in the default LLM SQLite database. You can add `--database /tmp/data.db` to specify an alternative location.

And now... I can run vibes-based semantic search against my codebase!

I could use the `llm similar` command for this, but I also have the ability to run these searches using Datasette itself.

Here’s a SQL query for that, using the [datasette-llm-embed](https://datasette.io/plugins/datasette-llm-embed) plugin from earlier:

```
with input as (
  select
    llm_embed(
      'sentence-transformers/TaylorAI/gte-tiny',
      :input
    ) as e
)
select
  id,
  content
from
  embeddings,
  input
where
  collection_id = (
    select id from collections where name = 'functions'
  )
order by
  llm_embed_cosine(embedding, input.e) desc
limit 5
```

The `:input` parameter is automatically turned into a form field by Datasette.

When I run this, I get back functions that relate to the concept of listing plugins:

![Running that query in Datasette with an input of list plugins returns the plugins() function from the cli.py file on line 175](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/list-plugins.jpg)

The key idea here is to use SQLite as an integration point—a substrate for combining together multiple tools.

I can run separate tools that extract functions from a codebase, run them through an embedding model, write those embeddings to SQLite and then run queries against the results.

Anything that can be piped into a tool can now be embedded and processed by the other components of this ecosystem.

#### Embedding text and images together using CLIP

My current favorite embedding model is [CLIP](https://openai.com/blog/clip/).

CLIP is a fascinating model released by OpenAI—back in January 2021, when they were still doing most things in the open—that can embed both text and images.

Crucially, it embeds them both into the same vector space.

If you embed the string “dog”, you’ll get a location in 512 dimensional space (depending on your CLIP configuration).

If you embed a photograph of a dog, you’ll get a location in that same space... and it will be close in terms of distance to the location of the string “dog”!

This means we can search for related images using text, and search for related text using images.

I built [an interactive demo](https://observablehq.com/@simonw/openai-clip-in-a-browser) to help explain how this works. The demo is an Observable notebook that runs the CLIP model directly in the browser.

It’s a pretty heavy page—it has to load 158MB of resources (64.6MB for the CLIP text model and 87.6MB for the image model)—but once loaded you can use it to embed an image, then embed a string of text and calculate the distance between the two.

I can give it this photo I took of a beach:

![A bright blue sky over a beach, with sandy cliffs and the Pacific ocean in the frame](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/beach.jpg)

Then type in different text strings to calculate a similarity score, here displayed as a percentage:

![Animation showing different similarity scores for different text strings](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/clip.gif)

| text             | score   |
| ---------------- | ------- |
| beach            | 26.946% |
| city             | 19.839% |
| sunshine         | 24.146% |
| sunshine beach   | 26.741% |
| california       | 25.686% |
| california beach | 27.427% |

It’s pretty amazing that we can do all of this in JavaScript running in the browser!

There’s an obvious catch: it’s not actually that useful to be able to take an arbitrary photo and say “how similar is this to the term ’city’?”.

The trick is to build additional interfaces on top of this. Once again, we have the ability to build vibes-based search engines.

Here’s a great example of one of those.

#### Faucet Finder: finding faucets with CLIP

[Drew Breunig](https://www.dbreunig.com/) used LLM and my [llm-clip](https://github.com/simonw/llm-clip) plugin to build a search engine for faucet taps.

He was renovating his bathroom, and he needed to buy new faucets. So he scraped 20,000 photographs of faucets from a faucet supply company and ran CLIP against all of them.

He used the result to build [Faucet Finder](https://faucet-finder.fly.dev/)—a custom tool (deployed using Datasette) for finding faucets that look similar to other faucets.

![The Faucet Finder homepage - six faucets, each with a Find Similar button.](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/faucet-finder.jpg)

Among other things, this means you can find an expensive faucet you like and then look for visually similar cheaper options!

Drew wrote more about his project in [Finding Bathroom Faucets with Embeddings](https://www.dbreunig.com/2023/09/26/faucet-finder.html).

Drew’s demo uses pre-calculated embeddings to display similar results without having to run the CLIP model on the server.

Inspired by this, I spent some time figuring out [how to deploy a server-side CLIP model](https://til.simonwillison.net/fly/clip-on-fly) hosted by my own [Fly.io](https://fly.io/) account.

Drew’s Datasette instance [includes this table](https://faucet-finder.fly.dev/faucets/embeddings) of embedding vectors, exposed via the Datasette API.

I deployed my own instance with [this API](https://clip-datasette-on-fly.fly.dev/_memory?sql=select+hex(llm_embed(%27clip%27%2C+%3Aq))+as+x&q=purple) for embedding text strings, then built an Observable notebook demo that hits both APIs and combines the results.

[observablehq.com/@simonw/search-for-faucets-with-clip-api](https://observablehq.com/@simonw/search-for-faucets-with-clip-api)

Now I can search for things like “gold purple” and get back vibes-based faucet results:

![Observable notebook: Search for Faucets with CLIP. The search term gold purple produces 8 alarmingly tasteless faucets in those combined colors.](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/clip-gold-purple.jpg)

Being able to spin up this kind of ultra-specific search engine in a few hours is exactly the kind of trick that excites me about having embeddings as a tool in my toolbox.

#### Clustering embeddings

Related content and semantic / vibes-based search are the two most comon applications of embeddings, but there are a bunch of other neat things you can do with them too.

One of those is clustering.

I built a plugin for this called [llm-cluster](https://github.com/simonw/llm-cluster) which implements this using [sklearn.cluster](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html) from scikit-learn.

To demonstrate that, I used my [paginate-json](https://github.com/simonw/paginate-json) tool and the GitHub issues API to collect the titles of all of the issues in my `simonw/llm` repository into a collection called `llm-issues`:

```
paginate-json 'https://api.github.com/repos/simonw/llm/issues?state=all&filter=all' \
  | jq '[.[] | {id: .id, title: .title}]' \
  | llm embed-multi llm-issues - \
  --store
```

Now I can create 10 clusters of issues like this:

```
llm install llm-cluster

llm cluster llm-issues 10
```

Clusters are output as a JSON array, with output that looks something like this (truncated):

```
[
  {
    "id": "2",
    "items": [
      {
        "id": "1650662628",
        "content": "Initial design"
      },
      {
        "id": "1650682379",
        "content": "Log prompts and responses to SQLite"
      }
    ]
  },
  {
    "id": "4",
    "items": [
      {
        "id": "1650760699",
        "content": "llm web command - launches a web server"
      },
      {
        "id": "1759659476",
        "content": "`llm models` command"
      },
      {
        "id": "1784156919",
        "content": "`llm.get_model(alias)` helper"
      }
    ]
  },
  {
    "id": "7",
    "items": [
      {
        "id": "1650765575",
        "content": "--code mode for outputting code"
      },
      {
        "id": "1659086298",
        "content": "Accept PROMPT from --stdin"
      },
      {
        "id": "1714651657",
        "content": "Accept input from standard in"
      }
    ]
  }
]
```

These do appear to be related, but we can do better. The `llm cluster` command has a `--summary` option which causes it to pass the resulting cluster text through a LLM and use it to generate a descriptive name for each cluster:

```
llm cluster llm-issues 10 --summary
```

This gives back names like “Log Management and Interactive Prompt Tracking” and “Continuing Conversation Mechanism and Management”. See [the README](https://github.com/simonw/llm-cluster/blob/main/README.md#generating-summaries-for-each-cluster) for more details.

#### Visualize in 2D with Principal Component Analysis

The problem with massively multi-dimensional space is that it’s really hard to visualize.

We can use a technique called Principal Component Analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the data to a more manageable size—and it turns out lower dimensions continue to capture useful semantic meaning about the content.

[Matt Webb](https://interconnected.org/) used the OpenAI embedding model to generate embeddings for descriptions of every episode of the BBC’s In Our Time podcast. He used these to find related episodes, but also ran PCA against them to create [an interactive 2D visualization](https://interconnected.org/more/2023/02/in_our_time-PCA-plot.html).

![Animated screenshot of a cloud of points in 2D space. At one side hovering over them shows things like The War of 1812 and The Battle of Trafalgar - at the other side we get Quantum Gravity and Higgs Boson and Carbon](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/cpa.gif)

Reducing 1,536 dimensions to just two still produces a meaningful way of exploring the data! Episodes about historic wars show up near each other, elsewhere there’s a cluster of episodes about modern scientific discoveries.

Matt wrote more about this in [Browse the BBC In Our Time archive by Dewey decimal code](https://interconnected.org/home/2023/02/07/braggoscope).

#### Scoring sentences using average locations

Another trick with embeddings is to use them for classification.

First calculate the average location for a group of embeddings that you have classified in a certain way, then compare embeddings of new content to those locations to assign it to a category.

Amelia Wattenberger demonstrated a beautiful example of this in [Getting creative with embeddings](https://wattenberger.com/thoughts/yay-embeddings-math).

She wanted to help people improve their writing by encouraging a mixture of concrete and abstract sentences. But how do you tell if a sentence of text is concrete or abstract?

Her trick was to generate samples of the two types of sentence, calculate their average locations and then score new sentences based on how close they are to either end of that newly defined spectrum.

![A document. Different sentences are displayed in different shades of green and purple, with a key on the right hand side showing that green means concreete and purple means abstract, with a gradient between them.](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2023/embeddings/amelia.jpg)

This score can even be converted into a color loosely representing how abstract or concrete a given sentence is!

This is a really neat demonstration of the kind of creative interfaces you can start to build on top of this technology.

#### Answering questions with Retrieval-Augmented Generation

I’ll finish with the idea that first got me excited about embeddings.

Everyone who tries out ChatGPT ends up asking the same question: how could I use a version of this to answer questions based on my own private notes, or the internal documents owned by my company?

People assume that the answer is to train a custom model on top of that content, likely at great expense.

It turns out that’s not actually necessary. You can use an off the shelf Large Language Model model (a hosted one or one that runs locally) and a trick called Retrieval Augmented Generation, or RAG.

The key idea is this: a user asks a question. You search your private documents for content that appears relevant to the question, then paste excerpts of that content into the LLM (respecting its size limit, usually between 3,000 and 6,000 words) along with the original question.

The LLM can then answer the question based on the additional content you provided.

This cheap trick is astonishingly effective. It’s trivial to get a basic version of this working—the challenge is in getting it to work as well as possible given the infinite set of questions a user might ask.

The key problem in RAG is figuring out the best possible excerpts of content to include in the prompt to the LLM.

“Vibes-based” semantic search powered by embedding is exactly the kind of thing you need to gather potentially relevant content to help answer a user’s question.

I built a version of this against content from my blog, described in detail in [Embedding paragraphs from my blog with E5-large-v2](https://til.simonwillison.net/llms/embed-paragraphs).

I used a model called [E5-large-v2](https://huggingface.co/intfloat/e5-large-v2) for this. It’s a model trained with this exact use-case in mind.

A challenge with finding content relevant to questions is that the user’s question—“What is shot-scraper?”—isn’t guaranteed to be considered semantically similar to content that answers that question. Questions and assertions have a different grammar from each other.

E5-large-v2 addresses this by supporting two types of content. You can embed phrases (factual sentences) and queries (questions) in the same space, similar to how CLIP supports both images and text.

I embedded 19,000 paragraphs of text from my blog as phrases, and now I can embed a question as a query and use that to find the paragraphs most likely to answer that question.

The result is RAG implemented as a one-liner Bash script:

```
llm similar blog-paragraphs -c "query: $1" \
  | jq '.content | sub("passage: "; "")' -r \
  | llm -m mlc-chat-Llama-2-7b-chat-hf-q4f16_1 \
  "$1" -s 'You answer questions as a single paragraph'
```

This example uses Llama 2 Chat 7B running on my laptop (with the [llm-mlc](https://github.com/simonw/llm-mlc) plugin), so I’m able to answer questions entirely offline using code running on my laptop.

Running this:

```
./blog-answer.sh 'What is shot-scraper?'
```

Outputs this:
> Shot-scraper is a Python utility that wraps Playwright, providing both a command line interface and a YAML-driven configuration flow for automating the process of taking screenshots of web pages and scraping data from them using JavaScript. It can be used to take one-off screenshots or take multiple screenshots in a repeatable way by defining them in a YAML file. Additionally, it can be used to execute JavaScript on a page and return the resulting value.

That’s a really good description of my [shot-scraper](https://shot-scraper.datasette.io/) tool. I checked and none of that output is an exact match to content I had previously published on my blog.

#### Q&A

My talk ended with a Q&A session. Here are the summarized questions and answers.

- **How does LangChain fit into this?**

    [LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/) is a popular framework for implementing features on top of LLMs. It covers a *lot* of ground—my only problem with LangChain is that you have to invest a lot of work in understanding how it works and what it can do for you. Retrieval Augmented Generation is one of the key features of LangChain, so a lot of the things I’ve shown you today could be built on top of LangChain if you invest the effort.

    My philosophy around this stuff differs from LangChain in that I’m focusing on building a suite of small tools that can work together, as opposed to a single framework that solves everything in one go.

- **Have you tried distance functions other than cosine similarity?**

    I have not. Cosine similarity is the default function that everyone else seems to be using and I’ve not spent any time yet exploring other options.

    I actually got ChatGPT to write all of my different versions of cosine similarity, across both Python and JavaScript!

    A fascinating thing about RAG is that it has so many different knobs that you can tweak. You can try different distance functions, different embedding models, different prompting strategies and different LLMs. There’s a lot of scope for experimentation here.

- **What do you need to adjust if you have 1 billion objects?**

    The demos I’ve shown today have all been on the small side—up to around 20,000 embeddings. This is small enough that you can run brute force cosine similarity functions against everything and get back results in a reasonable amount of time.

    If you’re dealing with more data there are a growing number of options that can help.

    Lots of startups are launching new “vector databases”—which are effectively databases that are custom built to answer nearest-neighbour queries against vectors as quickly as possible.

    I’m not convinced you need an entirely new database for this: I’m more excited about adding custom indexes to existing databases. For example, SQLite has [sqlite-vss](https://github.com/asg017/sqlite-vss) and PostgreSQL has [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector).

    I’ve also done some successful experiments with Facebook’s [FAISS](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss) library, including building a Datasette plugin that uses it called [datasette-faiss](https://datasette.io/plugins/datasette-faiss).

- **What improvements to embedding models are you excited to see?**

    I’m really excited about multi-modal models. CLIP is a great example, but I’ve also been experimenting with Facebook’s [ImageBind](https://github.com/facebookresearch/ImageBind), which “learns a joint embedding across six different modalities—images, text, audio, depth, thermal, and IMU data.” It looks like we can go a lot further than just images and text!

    I also like the trend of these models getting smaller. I demonstrated a new model, gte-tiny, earlier which is just 60MB. Being able to run these things on constrained devices, or in the browser, is really exciting to me.

#### Further reading

If you want to dive more into the low-level details of how embeddings work, I suggest the following:

- [What are embeddings?](https://vickiboykis.com/what_are_embeddings/) by Vicki Boykis
- [Text Embeddings Visually Explained](https://txt.cohere.com/text-embeddings/) by Meor Amer for Cohere
- [The Tensorflow Embedding Projector](https://projector.tensorflow.org/)—an interactive tool for exploring embedding spaces
- [Learn to Love Working with Vector Embeddings](https://www.pinecone.io/learn/) is a collection of tutorials from vector database vendor Pinecone

content.text:
In the brain, embeddings let an agent find facts by meaning when its question uses different words than the fact.

For example, the question "who's on call for pricing outages?" should find the fact "Pricing Platform supports the Rate Engine", even though they share almost no words. Text search misses that. Embedding search catches it.

message.content: Okay what changes are you going to make to the doc in this next revision? Also, help me understand the difference between options C and D for the implementation?

content.text:
**Changes for revision 3:**

1. Freshness follows the whole chain. A fact is stale if anything it cites, however many levels down, is stale.
2. The validator checks that each quote actually appears in its source.
3. A fact can be looked up directly, returning what it rests on and what rests on it.
4. Search in Phase 0 has two parts: exact lookup by name, alias, or symbol, and embeddings combined with text search for questions.
5. A new ingestion section, starting with how a code repo gets ingested.

**C versus D** comes down to where the knowledge is kept, and so what we have to build.

- **C:** knowledge lives as files in a git repo. Git already provides history, attribution, and rollback. We build only a small library that loads the files into memory to answer queries. That's fast to build, but weaker with many simultaneous writers and very large brains until we add a database index.
- **D:** knowledge lives in a database server. We build history, attribution, rollback, and search ourselves. That's stronger at scale and with concurrent writers, but it's weeks of work before you can use it.

C's Phase 2 adds a database too, but there the database is a rebuildable copy and git stays the original.

content.text:
It's simple for agents to use. It isn't simple to implement.

The six methods are easy to grasp. The hard part is the rules behind them, which every implementer would have to get right:

- **Freshness checks** for seven source types. Several of them need live access to Confluence, Slack, or git.
- **Transitive freshness** through fact-on-fact chains.
- **Contradiction clusters** returned in both directions.
- **The ownership rule**, plus rejecting `code:` predicates.
- **The derived code layer** from SCIP.

Compare a Message Board implementation, which mostly maps Slack's API. Here, an implementer would be building a storage engine and an accuracy engine.

The fix is to split it in two:

1. **A shared core** that Jive ships once. It handles freshness, validation, contradictions, ownership, and the code layer.
2. **A small storage interface** for implementers: save and load entities and facts, list by subject or object, and search. Roughly a database adapter.

Agents still see the same six methods. Someone new to the ecosystem then only writes the storage part, for example "the brain on Postgres", and the rules can't be implemented differently in each backend.

Do you expect multiple implementations? If there will only ever be one, this matters much less.

content.text:
Here's my understanding. The user defines a workflow, "Meeting summaries", and wires two interfaces into it:

- **MessageBoard**, implemented by Slack
- **KnowledgeGraph**, implemented by the brain

The workflow is triggered by a new message in `#meeting-transcripts`. The agent then works through these steps, calling only the APIs those interfaces expose:

1. **Read the transcript:** `messageBoard.getMessage(channel, ts)`.
2. **Resolve who and what is mentioned:** `knowledgeGraph.search("Acme")` and `search("Alex Leung")`, so existing entities are reused instead of duplicated.
3. **Check what's already known:** `knowledgeGraph.get("customer/acme")`, to spot facts the meeting confirms or contradicts.
4. **Write new facts:** `knowledgeGraph.write({ writer: "meeting-summarizer@1", rationale: "Summary of Acme sync 10/11", facts: [...] })`. Each fact cites `{ type: "message", ref: "slack://C123/171...", quote: "..." }`, and any conflicting fact sets `contradicts`.
5. **Post the summary:** `messageBoard.reply(channel, ts, summary)`.

The MessageBoard method names are my placeholders, because I haven't seen Jive's actual interface. The workflow never touches Slack's API or git directly, only the interfaces it was given.

message.content: Okay, and where does Jive's core come in to do the embeddings math? It doesn't there's no space for that. Please think critically when defining your interfaces

content.text:
You're right. I invented a layer Jive doesn't have. A workflow calls the interface, and the interface's implementation answers it. Nothing sits in between.

So everything has to live inside the implementation: embeddings, freshness, quote checks, contradictions, ownership, the code layer. Concretely:

- **The Convex component** implements the 6-method `KnowledgeGraph` interface and forwards each call over HTTP.
- **The brain service** behind it does all the work. It embeds text, runs searches, checks freshness, validates, and stores everything in git.

`BrainStore` then isn't part of Jive at all. At most it's an internal seam inside the brain service, so its storage could later move from git to Postgres.

That changes my answer on your earlier worry. New implementers wouldn't write a store against a Jive-provided core. They'd either point a component at the existing brain service, or reuse its logic as a library inside their own implementation. Which of those fits how Jive implementations normally get built?

content.text:
Fair. I kept bolting on mechanisms. Here's the simplest version I can defend.

**The brain stores sourced facts. Workflows keep it true.**

- **Implementation:** one service on one Postgres database. Entities, facts, and sources are rows. Text search and vector search are built into Postgres (pgvector). Facts are never edited in place. A new version supersedes the old one, which gives history and rollback without git.
- **Staleness, inverted:** the brain doesn't check seven external systems. The workflow that sees a change tells it: `sourceChanged("git:dat/rate-engine:src/retry.ts", "<new blob>")`. The brain marks every fact citing an older version stale, including facts that rest on those facts.
- **Code gets no special layer:** a "code indexer" workflow runs SCIP on each commit and writes `compiler-derived` facts like any other writer, replacing its previous ones.
- **The interface** is `write`, `retract`, `search`, `get`, `neighbors`, and `sourceChanged`.

That drops git as storage, the YAML files, the in-memory index, the derived code layer, the per-source freshness checkers, the CLI, and `BrainStore`.

Does that direction fit what you had in mind?

message.content: So you got rid of git and SCIP out of nowhere? It feels like we're going in circles now

content.text:
SCIP is still there. It just runs inside a code-indexer workflow instead of as a special layer in the brain. Git is still there as a source: facts cite commits and files. What I dropped is git as the brain's own storage, and I didn't give you the reason.

The reason: git was giving us history, attribution, and rollback. Append-only rows in a database give us the same three without the YAML files, index rebuilding, and merge conflicts.

You're right about the circles, though. I've been redesigning in response to each critique instead of reasoning from fixed requirements. I'd rather stop that: take the requirements as settled, and go through the major decisions one at a time with you, each justified only by a requirement. The first one is where the brain stores its data. Want to start there?

Here's where we are.

**Settled (from what you've told me):**

1. One brain per project, with code and business knowledge in one graph.
2. The KnowledgeGraph is a Jive interface. Workflows call it directly, and the implementation is a Convex component calling an external service.
3. Every fact has sources, a basis, a writer, and two timestamps: when the brain recorded it, and when the evidence is from.
4. Facts can cite other facts.
5. Conflicting facts coexist with their evidence. No claim categories; the reader judges.
6. The brain only flags stale facts. Workflows fix them.
7. Code structure comes from SCIP. No Sourcegraph, because of cost.
8. No read permissions. Writers can't alter each other's facts.
9. Search handles both exact names and meaning (embeddings).
10. Usable soon, at low cost.

**Open decisions:**

- **A. Storage:** git repo or Postgres with append-only rows.
- **B. Staleness detection:** the brain checks sources itself, or workflows report changes through `sourceChanged`.
- **C. Code facts:** written by an indexer workflow like any other facts, or computed live from SCIP indexes.
- **D.** The final list of interface methods, which follows from A through C.

**The doc:** revision 2 is out of date on B, C, D, and the "core" layer, which doesn't exist in Jive. I won't touch it until A through D are decided.

**Next:** decide A, one decision at a time, each justified only by the list above.
Okay. Getting back to an earlier question. What is the difference between these two?
[Image: source: /private/tmp/claude-502/-private-var-empty/afcf640b-3467-4bca-99a5-a127205f2e0a/images/1.png]

Both are services that implement the interface. The difference is where facts are stored, and so what we have to build.

**C. Brain-as-repo**
- Facts are stored as YAML text files in a git repo.
- Git provides history (commits), attribution (commit trailers), and rollback (`git revert`).
- We build parsing of those files into an in-memory index at startup, and search over that index.

**D. Custom**
- Facts are stored as rows in a database, for example Postgres.
- We build history (rows are never overwritten), attribution (a `writer` column), and rollback (retract rows by writer).
- Postgres provides text search and, through pgvector, vector search.

One correction to the doc's table. It says D takes weeks, but that assumed a Codex-sized D. The lean Postgres version I proposed earlier is option D, and I'd expect it to take about as long to build as C. That's my estimate, not something measured.

message.content: Models will work for hours on a project and believe it took weeks to build what it built

content.text:
Fair. My time estimates are human-engineer guesses, and they don't reflect how fast an agent builds. I'll drop build effort as a way of choosing between C and D.

On the merits:

- **D (Postgres)** handles many workflows writing at once, scales without rebuilding an index, and has text and vector search built in.
- **C (git repo)** gives you files a human can read, edit, and review in pull requests.

Since workflows, not people, will do most of the writing, I'd pick D. Do you want humans editing the brain directly?

message.content: D it is

content.text:
Next is decision B: how stale facts get detected.

1. **The brain checks sources itself.** It would need its own credentials for git, Confluence, Slack, and so on. That duplicates what Jive's other interfaces (MessageBoard, etc.) already provide to workflows.
2. **Workflows report changes.** A workflow that sees a change calls `sourceChanged(source, newVersion)`. The brain marks every fact citing an older version stale, plus every fact that cites those facts.

I recommend option 2. Workflows already have the triggers and the interfaces, and the brain stays free of connectors. The cost: a fact whose source no workflow watches never gets flagged. You'd fix that by adding a workflow for that source.

Option 2?

message.content: Jive handles credentials and integrates with message boards, task board, etc. Why on earth would a knowledge graph reach out to any of those things? Why would the knowledge graph even want to explicitly differentiate between those types of sources? There are infinite types of potential knowledge sources

content.text:
You're right on both counts. The brain should never contact anything; workflows bring it everything. And typed sources are another taxonomy I imposed. The brain doesn't need to know what a source *is*, only how to identify it and its version.

So the source type becomes generic:

```typescript
interface Source {
  ref: string;       // opaque identifier chosen by the writer, e.g. a URL or "git:dat/rate-engine:src/retry.ts"
  version: string;   // opaque; whatever identifies the evidence's state when cited
  at?: Timestamp;    // when the evidence was created
  quote?: string;    // exact supporting text
}
```

Facts that rest on other facts get their own field, `basedOn: { factId, revision }[]`, because that's the one kind of evidence the brain itself owns.

Staleness then needs only `sourceChanged(ref, version)`. The brain matches `ref` exactly and marks stale every fact citing a different version, plus anything `basedOn` those facts. That only works if every workflow writes the same `ref` for the same thing, so each interface should produce canonical refs for its objects.

lines: # Jive Knowledge Graph — Design
-**Status:** Draft for review, revision 2 · **Date:** 2026-10-10 · **Author:** Alex Leung (with Claude)
-**Supersedes:** `jive-memory-agent-handoff.md` (Codex, rev 0.2). Changes since revision 1 are listed in Appendix A.
+**Status:** Draft for review, revision 3 · **Date:** 2026-10-11 · **Author:** Alex Leung (with Claude)
+**Supersedes:** revision 2 and `jive-memory-agent-handoff.md`. Changes are listed in Appendix A.
-## 1. What we are building
+## 1. Summary

-Every Jive project gets one **brain**: a single body of knowledge that any agent working on the project can read and write. Its reader is a "super worker" who is staff engineer, designer, TPM, and CEO at once. That worker needs accurate knowledge of everything: how the code works, how the business works, who owns what, what was decided, what was promised, and what people intend to build.
+Each Jive project has one **brain**: a store of sourced facts about everything in the project, from code to customers. Workflows write facts into it and agents query it.
-The brain doesn't care what kind of project it serves:

+**The brain stores sourced facts. Workflows keep it true.** The brain never contacts Slack, git, Confluence, or anything else. Jive's other interfaces and workflows do that, and they tell the brain what they learn.
-| Project | Knowledge comes from | Example facts |
-| DAT (employer) | Code, Confluence, meetings, Slack, agent work | "Rate Engine computes lane rates via `computeRate`", "Pricing Platform owns Rate Engine", "We committed to customer A by Oct 23" |

-| Game decompilation (personal) | Original binary, decompiled C, subagent results | "Function `0x4012F0` matches byte for byte", "`Player` struct is 0x48 bytes", "`update_physics` calls `apply_gravity`" |
+## 2. How it fits into Jive

-The Knowledge Graph is a **Jive interface**, alongside Message Board (Slack, Discord) and Task Board (Linear, Jira). An implementation is a Convex component acting as a thin adapter over an external backend. This document specifies the interface and the recommended implementation.
+A Jive user builds workflows and wires interfaces into them. The Knowledge Graph is one interface, alongside Message Board and Task Board. Agents call the interfaces' methods.

-**One brain means one interface.** An agent asks the brain a question and gets one answer. Whether part of that answer was written by an agent, imported from a document, or computed from a compiler index is the implementation's concern. The agent sees it only as each fact's `basis` and `sources`.
+```text
+Workflow  ──calls──▶  KnowledgeGraph interface  ──implemented by──▶  Convex component
+                                                                       │ HTTP
+                                                                  brain service ── Postgres

-**Immediate use:** before Jive launches, Alex uses the brain standalone. Claude reads DAT code and documents and writes into it, and agents use skills to query it. Automated workflows (on commit, after meetings) come later and later move into Jive.
+Example: a meeting-summary workflow, with MessageBoard (Slack) and KnowledgeGraph wired in.
-## 2. Requirements
+1. Triggered by a new transcript posted in `#meeting-transcripts`.
+2. The agent reads the transcript through MessageBoard.
+3. `search("Acme")` finds the existing `customer/acme` entity, so the agent reuses it instead of creating a duplicate.
+4. `getEntity("customer/acme")` shows what's already known.
+5. `write(...)` adds new facts citing the transcript message and quoting it. Where the meeting contradicts an existing fact, the new fact lists it in `contradicts`.
+6. The agent posts a summary through MessageBoard.
-| # | Requirement | Why |

-| R1 | **One brain per project, domain-neutral,** with code and business knowledge in the same graph and linked to each other. | The super worker's questions cross domains: "which customer commitments touch code that this change affects?" |

-| R2 | **Every fact records its evidence, how it was derived, and when.** | Accuracy. Many agents write over time and some will be wrong. A claim without a source and a date can't be checked, weighed, or challenged. |

-| R3 | **Facts whose evidence has changed are detectable as possibly stale.** Agents and workflows do the fixing. The brain only points. | "Improve the graph on commit" requires knowing what the commit invalidated. |

-| R4 | **Conflicting claims coexist with their evidence.** Nothing is overwritten by whoever wrote last. | A Slack message can't override what the code does. "You're wrong, here's the code reference" has to win on evidence, not recency. |
-| R5 | **Code structure is compiler-exact,** not LLM-guessed. | "A calls B" is either true or false, and a compiler knows which. |

-| R6 | **Writers are attributed and contained.** One writer can't alter another's facts, and a writer's bad writes can be rolled back. | A misbehaving workflow shouldn't be able to corrupt the brain. |
-| R7 | **The interface reveals nothing about the backend.** | It's a Jive interface: implementations must be swappable, and agents shouldn't care how answers are produced. |
-| R8 | **Usable this week, at little to no cost.** | Alex needs to start building the DAT corpus now. A paid code-intelligence platform isn't affordable. |
+Example: a code workflow, triggered by a commit to a tracked repo.
-### Descriptive and normative claims
+1. For each changed file, call `sourceChanged("git:dat/rate-engine:src/retry.ts", "<new blob sha>")`. Every fact citing the old version is now stale.
+2. Run the SCIP indexer on the commit and `write` the resulting code facts (§4.4), retracting this workflow's previous facts for the changed files.
+3. `listFacts({ staleOnly: true, ... })` returns stale facts written by other workflows. The agent re-reads the code and updates or retracts its own, or flags others for the workflows that own them.

-Claims about a system can describe what it *does* ("retries use a fixed 5s delay"), what it *should* do ("retries should back off exponentially"), or what people *want* to build. Other useful slicings exist too: confirmed versus rumored, decision versus opinion, team scope versus company scope. No single taxonomy is the right one.
+## 3. Requirements
-**Decision:** the brain encodes no claim taxonomy and no rules about which evidence wins. Instead:
+| # | Requirement |
+| R1 | One brain per project. Code and business knowledge live in one graph. |
+| R2 | Every fact records its sources, how it was derived, who wrote it, and when. |
+| R3 | When a source changes, every fact that depends on it, directly or through other facts, is flagged stale. The brain flags; workflows fix. |
+| R4 | Conflicting facts coexist with their evidence. The brain never decides which is true. |
+| R5 | Code structure comes from a compiler (SCIP), not an LLM. |
+| R6 | A writer can change only its own facts. All history is kept, and one writer's changes can be reverted. |
+| R7 | Search finds things by exact name and by meaning. |
+| R8 | The brain never contacts external systems. |
+| R9 | A new implementer can read this document and build it. |
-- **Writers phrase claims accurately.** Normative claims say "should", "decided", or "plan to". This is a writing convention in `BRAIN.md`, not a schema field.

-- **Readers judge disagreements from the evidence.** An LLM reader can see that one claim cites the code and another cites a message saying the code is wrong. Guidance for readers lives in `BRAIN.md`, for example "code is authoritative on behavior, not on intent".

+**Non-goals:** read permissions (everyone using a project can read its whole brain), claim categories such as "intended" versus "current" (writers phrase claims accurately and readers judge), and source types (the brain treats every source as an opaque reference plus a version).
-If a specific kind of question turns out to be common and hard to answer this way, such as "where does reality diverge from what we intended?", a field can be added then, based on real use.
+## 4. Data model
-### Non-goals
-- **Read permissions.** In most companies, docs and code are broadly readable. Everything in a project's brain is visible to everyone using that project. The project boundary is the only wall.
-- **Truth adjudication.** The brain returns disagreements with their evidence and never picks a winner.
-- **Autonomous upkeep.** The brain never calls an LLM, crawls a source, or rewrites a fact by itself. Re-running compiler indexers on a new commit is the one exception, because it's mechanical.

-- **The Codex design's heavy machinery:** transitive atomic invalidation, snapshot publication, the three-clock temporal model, per-source ACLs, and one-container Postgres packaging. Each one served a requirement we don't have.
-## 3. Options considered
-### 3.1 Whole-brain backends

-**A. Graphiti** (open source, from Zep). A Python temporal knowledge graph framework. Per its README, it needs Neo4j, FalkorDB, or Neptune plus an LLM and embedding API. It ingests text "episodes" and uses an LLM to extract entities and edges. It has an MCP server and a REST service, and it automatically invalidates contradicted facts while keeping history.
-**B. Zep.** A managed service built on the Graphiti engine.
-**C. Brain-as-repo.** Written knowledge is stored as structured text in a git repository. Code structure is derived from SCIP indexes. A small library implements the interface over both (§6).
-**D. Custom database service.** Essentially a simplified Codex design.
-| Requirement | A. Graphiti | B. Zep | C. Brain-as-repo | D. Custom |
-| R1 one cross-linked brain | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
-| R2 evidence and time per fact | Partial: traces to episodes, not exact quotes or versions | Partial | **Yes**: explicit sources, plus git history | Yes |
-| R3 staleness from source changes | Its own temporal invalidation | Same | **Yes** (§5) | Yes |
-| R4 conflicts coexist | **Conflicts:** auto-invalidates contradicted facts. The exact mechanism needs verifying. | Same | **Yes** | Yes |
-| R5 compiler-exact code | No: LLM extraction | No | **Yes**: SCIP-derived layer | Yes, once built |
-| R6 attribution and rollback | Limited | Limited | **Yes**: one commit per write, revertible by writer | Yes, once built |
-| R8 this week, low cost | Yes, but one LLM call per write | Paid | **Yes** | **No**: weeks of work |
-| Writer controls exactly what's stored | No | No | **Yes** | Yes |
-| Multi-hop queries at scale | Strong | Strong | Adequate at first; Phase 2 index if needed | Strong |
-| Many concurrent writers | Good | Good | Serialized writer; fine for now | Good |
-### 3.2 Code layer: Sourcegraph versus self-hosted SCIP

-Sourcegraph is a code intelligence platform: cross-repo search, navigation through SCIP, an MCP server, and an LLM-driven "Deep Search". It only covers code and doesn't store written knowledge. Alex estimates the cost at about $16k; I haven't verified that. It's ruled out by R8.

-SCIP itself is an open protocol. Open-source indexers exist for Java/Scala/Kotlin, TypeScript/JavaScript, Rust, C/C++, Ruby, Python, C#/VB, Dart, and PHP, per the SCIP repository README. Go isn't listed there, so coverage needs checking. The `scip` CLI can print indexes as JSON and has an *experimental* SQLite export, which stores occurrences as opaque blobs. Bindings exist for Go, Rust, TypeScript, and Haskell. **Decision:** run the open-source indexers directly, and read their output through the TypeScript bindings inside the brain library.
-### 3.3 Recommendation
-**C. Brain-as-repo, with a SCIP-derived code layer and one interface over both.**
-1. **R4 rules out A and B as the system of record.** Their headline feature retires contradicted facts. Here, a Slack message must never be able to retire a code-backed fact.
-2. **R2 and R5 favor exact writes over LLM extraction.** Accuracy is the brain's value, and passing every write through another model's interpretation adds an unaccountable source of error.
-3. **Git provides most of what the Codex design hand-built:** immutable history, attribution, diffs, time travel, and revert.
-4. **No lock-in.** Agents only ever see the interface. If scale demands it, Phase 2 adds a database index rebuilt from the repo, and the repo stays the source of truth.
-## 4. Logical model
-This section is what agents and the interface see. Storage is covered in §7.
### 4.1 Entities
-An entity is anything worth knowing about: a person, team, customer, service, decision, commitment, process, concept, function, or struct.
+An entity is anything facts can be about: a person, team, customer, service, decision, function, and so on.

-- **IDs are stable strings, opaque to callers.** Written entities use readable IDs like `service/rate-engine`. Code entities use `scip:<SCIP symbol>`. An ID never changes. If a name changes, the entity's `name` changes and its ID stays.
-- **Types are free strings,** with a recommended vocabulary in `BRAIN.md`. There's no hard-coded domain model.
-- **An entity record holds only its ID, type, name, and aliases.** Everything else known about it, including its summary, is a fact with sources. An entity with no sourced facts is invalid.
-- **Names are not identities.** Two entities that may be the same are linked by a sourced `same-as` fact, never merged by name.
+```typescript
+interface Entity {
+  id: EntityId;       // stable, never changes. Examples: "customer/acme", "scip:<SCIP symbol>"
+  type: string;       // free text. Examples: "person", "service", "function"
+  name: string;
+  aliases: string[];  // other names, used by exact-name search

+Any writer may create an entity or update its name and aliases. Entity changes are kept in history. IDs are chosen by writers. By convention, written entities use `<type>/<slug>`, and code symbols use `scip:` plus their SCIP symbol string.
### 4.2 Facts
-A fact is a sourced claim about one subject entity. It either points at another entity (`object`) or states a literal (`value`). Prose such as a summary is a fact whose predicate is `summary`.
+A fact is one claim about one subject entity. It either links to another entity (`object`) or states a value (`value`).
-| Field | Meaning |
-| `id` | Unique, never reused. |
-| `subject` | Entity the fact is about. |
-| `predicate` | Free string with a recommended vocabulary. The `code:` namespace is reserved for derived facts (§4.3). |
-| `object` / `value` | Exactly one: an entity ID, or a literal value. |
-| `basis` | `compiler-derived`, `imported`, `human-asserted`, or `model-inferred`. A label for readers, not proof. |
-| `writer` | Agent, workflow, or indexer identity plus version. |
-| `recordedAt` | When the brain learned this fact. Set by the implementation. |
-| `revision` | Changes whenever the fact is edited or retracted. Used by facts that cite other facts. |
-| `sources` | One or more pieces of exact evidence (§5.1), each with its own timestamp `at`. |
-| `contradicts` | Optional IDs of facts this one disputes. Both remain. |
-| `status` | `active` or `retracted` (with a reason). |
+```typescript
+interface Source {
+  ref: string;        // opaque ID of the evidence, chosen by the writer, e.g. "slack:C123/1728400000.123"
+  version: string;    // opaque version of the evidence at the time it was cited
+  at?: Timestamp;     // when the evidence was created (message time, commit time, ...)
+  quote?: string;     // exact text from the evidence that supports the fact

-**Two timestamps, on purpose.** `recordedAt` is when the brain learned something. A source's `at` is when the evidence itself came into being. A two-year-old message written into the brain today is still two-year-old evidence. There are deliberately no "valid from / valid until" ranges. When a claim really is time-bound ("until Q3", "due Oct 23"), the fact says so in its value.
+interface Fact {
+  id: FactId;
+  revision: string;           // changes every time the fact is updated or retracted
+  subject: EntityId;
+  predicate: string;          // free text, e.g. "owned-by", "retry-behavior", "code:references"
+  object?: EntityId;          // exactly one of object / value is set
+  value?: Json;
+  basis: 'compiler-derived' | 'imported' | 'human-asserted' | 'model-inferred';
+  writer: WriterId;           // set by the service from the caller's credentials
+  recordedAt: Timestamp;      // when this revision was written
+  sources: Source[];          // external evidence
+  basedOn: { factId: FactId; revision: string }[];  // other facts this one rests on
+  contradicts: FactId[];      // facts this one disputes; both stay
+  status: 'active' | 'retracted';
+  retractedReason?: string;
-**Ownership rule (R6):** a writer may edit or retract only its own facts. To dispute another writer's fact, it adds a new fact with `contradicts`. Humans may edit anything.
+Rules:
-### 4.3 Written facts and derived facts
+- A fact needs at least one entry in `sources` or `basedOn`.
+- `basedOn` and `contradicts` may only reference existing facts. `basedOn` may not form a cycle.
+- Facts are never edited in place. An update creates a new revision, and old revisions stay readable.
-The brain has two kinds of facts, and the interface treats them the same way:
+### 4.3 Staleness
-| | Written facts | Derived facts |
-| Produced by | Agents, workflows, humans | Compiler indexers (SCIP) on tracked repos |
-| Examples | Ownership, intent, decisions, commitments, explanations, known bugs | `code:defines`, `code:references`, `code:calls`, `code:implements` |
-| `basis` | Any except `compiler-derived` | `compiler-derived` |
-| Changes when | A writer edits or retracts it | The tracked repo's head changes and the indexer re-runs |
-| Can go stale? | Yes (§5) | No. Always reflects the indexed commit. |
-| Stored? | Yes | No. Computed from the current index. |
+The service keeps one record per source `ref`: the latest version reported through `sourceChanged`. A fact is **stale** if any of these is true:

-So `get("scip:… computeRate().")` returns the function's definition location, its derived references and calls, and every written fact about it, such as who owns it and its known bugs. `neighbors` from `customer/acme` can follow a written `depends-on` fact to `service/rate-engine`, then a written `implemented-by` fact to a code symbol, then derived `code:calls` edges, all in one traversal. Writers may *cite* code symbols, but may not *write* `code:` predicates.
+1. One of its `sources` has a reported latest version that differs from the version the fact cites.
+2. A fact in its `basedOn` is stale, retracted, or has a newer revision than the one cited.

-The derived layer is generic. SCIP is the first provider because it covers most languages. For the decompilation project, decompiled C is indexed with `scip-clang`, and results about the binary (match status, sizes) are written facts with `artifact` sources. A project without code simply has no derived layer, and nothing in the interface changes.
+Rule 2 applies recursively, so a conclusion is stale if anything beneath it is.
-## 5. Accuracy mechanics

+A ref that has never been reported through `sourceChanged` has no latest version, and facts citing it are not stale. Versions are opaque and can't be ordered, so a workflow that observes a new version should call `sourceChanged` before writing facts that cite it.
-### 5.1 Sources
+A stale fact becomes fresh again when its writer updates it to cite the current versions.
-| `type` | Identifies | Version recorded | Freshness check |
-| `git` | repo, path, optional line range | commit plus file blob SHA | The blob at the tracked head differs, or the path is gone, so the fact is stale. |
-| `symbol` | SCIP symbol, repo | commit plus blob of the defining file | The symbol is gone from the current index, or its defining file's blob changed, so the fact is stale. |
-| `doc` | Confluence page, Google Doc, etc. | page version or last-modified | Compare through the system's API when a connector exists. Otherwise `unverifiable`. |
-| `message` | platform, channel, message timestamp | original or edit time | Usually immutable. Check edits where the platform exposes them. |
-| `meeting` | transcript ID and segment | transcript revision | Compare revisions. |
-| `artifact` | binary, build output, test report | content hash | Compare hashes. |
-| `fact` | another fact's ID | that fact's `revision` | Stale if the cited fact changed or was retracted. One hop only, not a transitive cascade. |
+### 4.4 Code facts

-Every source has an `at` timestamp: commit date, message time, meeting date, or document version date. It's filled in automatically when the source carries one, and the validator warns when it's missing. Every source may also carry a `quote`, the exact text the claim rests on, so readers can verify without fetching.
+Code is not special. A code-indexer workflow runs the SCIP indexer for a repo and writes ordinary facts with `basis: 'compiler-derived'`:

-**File-level checks are deliberately conservative.** An unrelated edit elsewhere in a cited file also flags the fact. A false "maybe stale" costs an agent one re-check. A missed stale fact costs accuracy.
+- One entity per symbol: `id: "scip:<symbol>"`, `type` from SCIP's symbol kind.
+- Facts such as `code:defined-in` and `code:references`, each citing `ref: "git:<repo>:<path>"` with the file's blob SHA as `version`.
-### 5.2 Staleness is computed, not stored

+The exact predicate set must follow the relationships SCIP actually emits; see `scip.proto` in the SCIP repository. Other writers' facts can link to code entities. For example, `service/rate-engine` `implemented-by` `scip:…`.

-There's no stale flag to keep in sync. Every read returns `freshness: fresh | stale | unverifiable` per fact, computed from the checks above. `stale(scope)` lists stale facts for a repo, document, or the whole brain. After a commit lands, a workflow re-runs the indexer for that repo, calls `stale({ scope: "repo:<name>" })`, and re-derives what it finds. That's the "improve the graph on commit" loop.
+## 5. Interface
-### 5.3 Contradictions
+All methods are called by workflows' agents. The caller's identity, its `WriterId`, comes from its credentials, never from method arguments.

-A read that returns a fact also returns every fact linked to it by `contradicts`, in either direction, with full sources. The brain doesn't rank, filter, or order a cluster by truth. Judging it is the reader's job, using the evidence and the guidance in `BRAIN.md`.
-## 6. The Jive Knowledge Graph interface
```typescript
-export type EntityId = string;   // opaque, stable: "service/rate-engine", "scip:<symbol>"
-export type WriterId = string;   // e.g. "claude/dat-reader@1", "scip-typescript@0.3"
-export type Timestamp = string;  // ISO 8601, UTC
-export type Json = null | boolean | number | string | Json[] | { [k: string]: Json };
+type EntityId = string;
+type FactId = string;
+type WriterId = string;     // e.g. "workflow/meeting-summary@1"
+type Timestamp = string;    // ISO 8601, UTC
+type Json = null | boolean | number | string | Json[] | { [k: string]: Json };
-export type Source = { at?: Timestamp; quote?: string } & (
-  | { type: 'git'; repo: string; path: string; commit: string; blob: string; lines?: [number, number] }
-  | { type: 'symbol'; symbol: string; repo: string; commit: string; blob: string }
-  | { type: 'doc' | 'message' | 'meeting' | 'artifact'; ref: string; version: string; locator?: Record<string, string> }
-  | { type: 'fact'; factId: string; revision: string }
-export interface Fact {
-  id: string;
-  subject: EntityId;
-  predicate: string;
-  object?: EntityId;              // exactly one of object / value
-  value?: Json;
-  basis: 'compiler-derived' | 'imported' | 'human-asserted' | 'model-inferred';
-  writer: WriterId;
-  recordedAt: Timestamp;
-  revision: string;
-  sources: Source[];              // at least one

+Errors: `INVALID_INPUT` (bad shape, missing evidence, cycle, unknown reference), `NOT_OWNER` (changing another writer's fact), `CONFLICT` (`revision` doesn't match the current one), `NOT_FOUND`.

-- **Nothing reveals the backend.** IDs aren't file paths, results return a `revision` rather than a git commit, and code facts arrive as ordinary facts with `basis: compiler-derived`.
-- **No delete.** Retraction keeps history. Humans can still hard-remove material from the store for genuine mistakes or sensitive data.
-- **Caller identity.** In Phase 0 the caller declares its `writer`. Phase 1 binds `writer` to the caller's credential so one agent can't impersonate another.
